entry.title: Patrizia Rossi
entry.content:
More about Patrizia in SAP Community

LinkedIn

 

Location (City, Country): Rome, Italy 
Occupation: SAP Solution Architect at the European Space Agency

 


Patrizia, tell us about yourself.
Who are you, what do you like to do, what is important to you?

I was born in Rome, and ever since I was a child, I dreamt of becoming a programmer because of my love for computers. Technology fascinates me, especially home automation, but I also enjoy playing sports with my dog, Joker. For me, it's crucial to always believe in dreams and find ways to make them come true.


What is your area of expertise?
What does a usual day at work look like for you?

I started my career many years ago developing in ABAP, and it's still my first love, I've never really put it down. Over the years I specialised in SAP Fiori and then SAP BTP, and today I work as an SAP Solution Architect across the whole platform: foundation and platform services, CAP, Fiori, and increasingly the AI and agentic side with Joule. I work inside an IT team, and what I enjoy most is taking a solution end to end, sitting with the business to understand what they actually need, designing the architecture, and staying with it all the way to the code: sometimes I develop it myself, sometimes my analysis is what someone else builds from. Colleagues often come to me when something new comes up, because they know I'll have looked into it. This platform changes constantly, and I spend a lot of my time studying what's coming next


What inspired you to become an SAP Champion in SAP Community?

Ever since my early years in the SAP Community, I have always found great inspiration in the SAP Mentors. I've always admired them, and thanks to various events, I had the opportunity to meet some of them in person. Now, being an SAP Champion feels like fulfilling a dream. Knowing that I am part of a vast community and can contribute to its growth, even in a small way, is a wonderful feeling.


How do you learn in SAP Community?
What is your daily/weekly routine in SAP Community?

When I first joined the SAP Community, my goal was to find solutions to the technical problems I faced in my programming career. Gradually, I began to feel more involved, especially through organizing SAP Inside Track events and similar activities. Now, my use of the community has evolved to include interacting with other members, seeking advice, and sharing suggestions. Of course, I also continue to search for solutions to technical challenges.


What is your suggestion to get the most out of SAP Community?

To get the most out of the SAP Community, I believe it's truly beneficial to participate in initiatives such as Inside Track events, CodeJam, and similar activities. These events provide opportunities to meet the gurus who write the blogs, build strong relationships, and always have great points of reference. It's these connections and interactions that enrich your experience in the community.

Patrizia's question to you:
MMhh, I don't have a specific question, but over the years, I've noticed a scarcity of Italian women in the SAP Community. Do you think there's a way I could encourage more of them to become a part of the community? Could I be a good example for them?

entry.title: Over your FUE entitlement in RISE with SAP? It is fixable, and it is not a role redesign project
entry.content:
You may be reading this because a monthly measurement came back above your contracted entitlement. Perhaps several have. Perhaps an email has already arrived asking you to schedule a conversation about the gap, or an adjustment to your subscription volume has been put on the table.

If so, the first thing worth saying is that this is common, it is rarely evidence that anything was done wrong, and it is usually fixable with a number of changes you can count on one hand. No role concept redesign. No change to how a single employee does their job.

The second is that the clock matters far more than the invoice suggests, and the reason is not obvious.

Why the number got high

Under RISE with SAP, user licensing is measured in Full Use Equivalents, and the measurement is driven by the authorization content assigned to each user, not by what that user actually does in the system.

That second figure has a name in the measurement data: active usage, the record of which transactions and services each user has actually executed over an observation window. Both numbers are available. Most teams have only ever looked at the first.

Three properties of the model combine into a slow ratchet.

It is authorization-based. Classification follows the objects and values a user holds. Whether they ever execute the corresponding function is not part of the calculation.

It is ceiling-based. A single value mapping to a higher band promotes the entire user to that band. It does not matter that the rest of their profile is display-only, that the value arrived through a composite role, or that they hold no transaction from which the check could even be triggered.

Role content only ever accumulates. Roles get copied when a new team needs something similar. Templates carry values nobody examined. A capability is added for a go-live and never removed. Nothing in normal operations takes authorization away, so the authorization-based figure drifts upward year after year while active usage stays flat or declines.

Put those together and a landscape running perfectly well, supporting a business that has not materially changed, quietly consumes more every measurement cycle. Nobody made a mistake. The model simply has no self-correcting mechanism.

Why the clock matters more than the invoice

This is the part that gets misjudged most often, and it is worth being precise about.

Under a typical RISE agreement, consumption is measured monthly, but the invoice follows the contracted subscription rather than the measurement. A month of overconsumption does not arrive as a larger bill. Which is exactly why it tends to get filed under "look at it next quarter".

What sustained overconsumption does trigger is a conversation, and normally a defined period in which to bring consumption back inside entitlement. If it is not resolved within that period, the contracted volume is adjusted upward, and that adjustment applies for the remainder of the term. On a standard three-year agreement, that can mean a long time.

Here is the consequence people miss: the adjustment does not unwind. Reducing consumption after the higher volume has been contracted does not reduce what you pay for the rest of the term. You end up paying for an entitlement you have demonstrably stopped needing.

So there are two windows, and it is worth knowing which one you are in.

The remediation window. Between the gap being raised and a volume adjustment being agreed. This is where the leverage is, and it is measured in months, not years. Consumption brought back inside entitlement here costs nothing extra at all.

The renewal window. If an adjustment has already been made, the next genuine opportunity is renewal. What carries weight in that conversation is not a projection or a remediation plan. It is a run of recent monthly measurements showing that consumption is genuinely and sustainably lower. That record takes months to accumulate, which means the optimisation work has to be finished well before negotiations begin, not during them.

One more thing worth doing in either window. Establish independently what your own active usage justifies, before agreeing to any number. That figure comes out of your own system, it is the floor the analysis is working toward, and it is the only number in the conversation that is not somebody's estimate.

So "it is too late" is almost never the right conclusion. "We will look at it after the busy period" very often is the expensive one.

Contract terms vary considerably. Check how your own agreement handles measurement, remediation periods and volume adjustment rather than relying on the general shape described here.

What the gap is typically worth

The published conversion ratios do the heavy lifting.

Classification Ratio

Advanced Use1 user = 1 FUE
Core Use5 users = 1 FUE
Self-Service Use30 users = 1 FUE

Ratios applicable to any given customer are those in their RISE agreement and should be read from that document where they differ.

An illustration. Take 200 users classified Advanced Use by their authorization content, which is 200 FUE. Suppose active usage justifies Advanced Use for 30 of them, Core Use for 120, and Self-Service for 50. That same population, correctly classified, consumes roughly 56 FUE.

The arithmetic is dramatic because the ratios are non-linear. Moving one user from Advanced to Core releases 0.8 FUE. Moving them to Self-Service releases 0.97. Across a few dozen users the numbers get large quickly.

 FIGURE 1 FUE Gap | Authorization vs Active Use. The two numbers side by side in a live system. Authorization content drives 182 FUE. Active usage justifies 20. The breakdown underneath shows where the gap sits, which is almost entirely in the Advanced Use band. A view like this takes minutes to produce and tells you, before you commit anyone to anything, whether the exercise is worth staffing.

Two qualifications, because overpromising here helps nobody. The theoretical gap is never fully reachable. Some users hold a higher-band role that genuinely cannot be reduced, and the ceiling effect means others are blocked by roles outside your change scope. Part of the population is also correctly classified already. A realistic target sits between the two figures, and establishing where is the first job of any serious analysis.

Why the fix is smaller than the problem

Here is the part that surprises people, and the reason this does not need to be a programme.

Because measurement is ceiling-based, the damage concentrates. A single unused authorization value sitting in one widely assigned role can hold hundreds of users in the top band on its own. Remove that one value and every user held there only by it drops immediately.

The inverse is what makes the work tractable. You do not need to clean up the whole authorization model to move the number. You need to find the specific values doing the promoting, confirm nobody is exercising them, and take them out. In most landscapes that is a handful of values across a handful of roles.

This is why the response to an overconsumption notice should not be an authorization redesign.

  Authorization model redesign Targeted FUE reduction

ScopeThe whole role conceptOnly the roles driving classification
DurationMonths, often longerWeeks
Business testingFull regression across processesLimited to the affected check surface
User impactRetraining and reassignment at scaleMost users unaffected entirely
ReversibilityDifficult once underwayPer change, per transport
Cost profileProgrammeShort engagement

A redesign may well be justified for other reasons such as segregation of duties, audit findings or technical debt. But it is a poor instrument for a licensing problem, it is slow precisely when the remediation window is running, and it disrupts people who were never the cause.

Why per-role optimisation potential misleads you

Good tooling will rank your roles by optimisation potential: which roles carry values in a band above Self-Service, how many values sit in each band, and how many users hold the role.

FIGURE 2 op 10 Roles with the Highest Optimization Potential. Roles ranked by optimisation potential, showing how many authorization values fall into each classification band and how many users hold each role. The top two rows carry a single Advanced-classified value apiece, and reach 108 and 105 users. That is where to look first. It is not yet a saving.

That view is genuinely useful, and it is where the work starts. Look at the top two rows in particular. One Advanced-classified authorization value, in a role assigned to over a hundred users. That is the concentration effect from the previous section, visible in a single line, and it is the reason a small number of changes can move a large number.

But it is a candidate list, not a forecast, and treating it as a forecast is the most common way this work loses credibility. Two things stand between the potential and the saving.

The value may be in use. The ranking counts authorization values. It says nothing about whether anybody executes them. Until active usage has been measured across the full check surface for that specific value, a high-potential role is a hypothesis rather than a finding.

The ceiling has to clear. Even where the value is provably unused, a user changes band only when every role they hold has been addressed. Of those hundred-plus users, any who also hold a second Advanced-classified role will not move at all when this one is fixed. Your carefully evidenced change measures as zero, and it looks like the analysis was wrong.

So read a ranking like this as a work queue ordered by what is at stake, not as a list of savings waiting to be collected. It tells you where to look first. It does not tell you what you will get.

That distinction is the single largest source of disappointment in this work. If you have committed to the per-role number in a remediation conversation, it is also the most expensive.

It is also the strongest argument for simulating a change before specifying it. Model the change, re-run the measurement against the simulated state, and you find out whether the ceiling actually cleared before anyone writes a transport.

A six-step test per candidate

  1. Identify the driving value. Which authorization object, field and value in the role maps to a band above Self-Service.

  2. Establish the complete check surface. Which standard transactions and services actually execute the check for that specific value. The system's own authorization check defaults give you this. The emphasis on the specific value matters, because the surface for a single activity is far narrower than the surface for the object as a whole, and using the wider list will make a safe change look dangerous.

  3. Measure active usage across that surface for every user in the system, not only the role's holders. Workload statistics and single-record statistics both, since their coverage differs.

  4. Verify residual coverage. Confirm the authorization business users actually rely on, typically Display, exists in the same authorization and survives the change.

  5. Test the ceiling. Confirm each affected user holds no other role carrying a value in the same band.

  6. Quantify. Users reclassified, and the resulting movement in measured consumption.

This sequence is also what protects your users. A change only reaches a transport when active usage shows nobody affected is exercising the value, and when display and reporting capability is confirmed to survive. Done properly, nobody notices anything changed, which is the point.

Where evidence does not settle a question, and seasonal transactions falling outside the observation window are the classic case, record it as a named open point and take it to the process owner. Do not resolve it by assumption.

Two shapes of change, handled differently

Single-touch. Nobody in the system exercises the value. Remove it in place. No role gets rebuilt, no user assignment changes, and the risk is minimal because no active usage anywhere in the system is about as strong as evidence gets. These are fast and typically carry most of the early reduction.

Cohort-based. The value is genuinely exercised, but only by some holders. Here the role cannot be stripped. Split the population by active usage, build a replacement role without the value, and move only the users with none. Slower, more testing, and this is where the ceiling work concentrates. It also reaches users that single-touch changes cannot.

Getting the categorisation wrong is expensive both ways. Strip a role people actually use and you generate incidents. Build a replacement role where an in-place removal would have done and you have created a reassignment project for nothing.

Why this is slow by hand

The analysis is a join across four datasets, repeated for every candidate:

  1. Consumption and classification, per user, by authorization and by active usage
  2. Role, profile and authorization object content
  3. Authorization check defaults, meaning which transactions and services check which object and value
  4. Active usage, per user, per object, over the observation window

No single one answers a question. Every conclusion requires moving between all four, then doing it again for the next candidate, and again after each simulated change to see whether the ceiling actually cleared.

Through manual extraction and spreadsheet reconciliation, one candidate role is a half-day. A few hundred roles becomes a multi-month engagement, and the natural response of sampling rather than testing exhaustively is exactly what produces per-role forecasts that later fail to materialise. If you are inside a remediation window, a multi-month engagement is also simply the wrong shape.

The constraint is not analytical difficulty. It is loop speed.

Where agentic analysis changes the economics

This suits an agentic approach for a specific reason. The work is not one hard question. It is several hundred easy questions that must be asked in the right order, each answer determining the next.

Exposing the four datasets through an MCP server turns them into tools an agent can query directly. Consumption figures, role and authorization content, check defaults and active usage all become callable, so the agent can traverse the chain without a human copying data between systems at each hop.

 FIGURE 3 the Accelerator for SAM4U Adoption connected as an MCP connector, tool permissions view. Eighteen measurement datasources exposed as tools the agent can call directly. Between them they cover the four datasets above: consumption and classification per user, role and profile content, authorization object values, the classification ruleset, and active usage. Nothing has to be extracted or reconciled by hand first.

From there the agent works the chain: consumption figure, to driving value, to check surface, to active usage evidence, to ceiling test. Candidates that will not hold get discarded in minutes instead of surviving until someone writes a change document for them.

 FIGURE 4 cohort analysis session, working a single candidate rol. One candidate worked through in the chat. The agent identifies the role's only Advanced-classified value, recognises it as the same object it had already analysed in a different role, recalls that the object's entire check surface has no active usage anywhere in the system, and moves straight to retrieving the role's holders for the ceiling test. Each answer determines the next query, and the loop runs in minutes rather than days.

The critical part is that the traversal is not improvised. The methodology above, packaged as a skill the agent follows, is what makes the output auditable rather than merely plausible. An agent with data access and no method will produce confident, well-formatted, wrong answers. The method is the product. Tool access is what makes it fast.

Model choice is a data residency decision

Authorization content is sensitive. Role names, object values and user assignments map your segregation of duties and your soft spots. Many organisations, and public sector bodies and regulated utilities in particular, cannot send that to a commercial model API. No efficiency argument will move them.

So the model tier has to be a customer decision rather than an architectural assumption.

Premium hosted models such as Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, where governance permits external processing. Strongest reasoning, and the best handling of long multi-step analysis chains.

Self-hosted open-weight models such as the Gemma and GPT-OSS families and their equivalents, running inside the customer's own boundary, where nothing leaves. A lower ceiling on complex reasoning, but for a well-specified methodology with clearly defined steps, that ceiling is rarely the binding constraint.

Both work. The method does not change. Only where inference happens does. Designing for both is the difference between something a regulated customer can adopt and something they will admire from a distance.

Where our accelerator fits

Skybuffer's Accelerator for SAM4U Adoption is published on the SAP Store. It builds on SAM4U, the standard measurement capability SAP provides to RISE customers, and adds three things: reporting and dashboarding over the measurement data, simulation so a change can be modelled before it touches a system, and MCP server interfaces that make the datasets available to an AI agent, hosted or self-hosted, per the customer's governance.

Packaged with it is the methodology described here, as a skill the agent follows. That combination is the point. Experienced consultants know which questions to ask and which answers to distrust. Large models can execute that inquiry across hundreds of roles at a speed no manual process matches. Neither half suffices alone. An expert without tooling runs out of hours, and a model without a method produces analysis that reads well and does not survive re-measurement.

Accelerator for SAM4U Adoption on the SAP Store: https://www.sap.com/products/technology-platform/partners/skybuffer-as-accelerator-for-sam4u-adoption.html

If you are over today, four things to do this week

Find out which window you are in. Has a volume adjustment been agreed, or is there still a remediation period running? The answer changes the entire shape of the response, and it is a question for your commercial team rather than your Basis team.

Pull both numbers. Authorization-based consumption and the consumption active usage justifies. The gap between them is your realistic ceiling, it tells you within a day whether this is a small exercise or a large one, and it gives you a floor that came out of your own system rather than somebody's estimate.

Resist the redesign reflex. The instinct after an overconsumption notice is to announce a programme. Find the driving values first. The fix is usually far smaller than the problem feels, and you can always redesign later for reasons that actually warrant it.

Test the ceiling before committing to a figure. Per-role potential is a candidate list. Users move when every role they hold moves, and promising the per-role number in a conversation with your account team is how a credible position stops being credible.

Disclosure: I work for Skybuffer AS, an SAP partner. The Accelerator for SAM4U Adoption referenced above is our product. The method described here is not specific to it and can be applied with any tooling that reaches the underlying measurement data.

Happy to take questions in the comments, particularly on ceiling testing, which is where most of the surprises live.

entry.title: Your ABAP backlog is not a capacity problem. We gave the AI toolchain to consultants, not developers
entry.content:
Two weeks later, for the first time in the company's history, we did not have enough tasks to fill the ABAP developer queue.

For years we had the same problem every SAP shop has. Not enough ABAP capacity. A queue of business requirements that never got shorter. Recruitment that never quite closed the gap, because senior ABAP people are scarce and expensive, and because the mid-level people you can actually hire need supervision from the senior people you could not hire.

We worked on this for a long time, and we worked on it hard. We tried a great deal, and for most of that time we treated it as a productivity problem, which is what everyone does. Make the developers faster. Give them better completion, better refactoring, better generation. Every one of those attempts produced something real, and none of them made the queue shorter.

Eventually we stopped and asked a different question: who is actually waiting?

The answer was not the developer. The developer was busy. The thing that was waiting was the requirement, and it was waiting in the gap between the person who understood it and the person who could implement it.

Reaching that conclusion took far longer than implementing it. Once we accepted it, we moved the tooling across that gap and gave it to the consultants.

That took two weeks. Nothing about our developers changed in those two weeks. Same people, same skills, same system. What changed was who started the work, and how much context survived before it started.

This article describes what we built, what it cost us to get there, what it does not do, and what we measured.

The bottleneck was never typing speed

Consider what happens to an ordinary custom requirement in an ordinary SAP project.

A business user describes what they need to a functional consultant. The consultant understands it, because the consultant sits close to the business and knows how this particular company has configured and extended SAP. The consultant writes it down. That document goes to a developer, who knows the system deeply but was not in the room and does not carry the business context. Meetings follow. The developer builds something. The consultant tests it, finds the three things the specification did not quite say, and explains again. Another round. Then another.

None of that is anybody's fault. It is a structural property of how the work is divided. Every hop across that boundary loses fidelity, and the loss is recovered through iteration, which is expensive and slow.

The second structural problem is testing. A developer often cannot meaningfully test what they built, because a real test needs business data, a business process and a judgement about whether the result is right. That judgement lives with the consultant. So the developer builds, hands over, waits, and then context-switches back days later to fix it.

Neither problem is solved by making the developer type faster. Both are solved by removing the hop.

What the rest of the industry is building right now

There is a lot of good work happening on AI-assisted ABAP development, and much of it is built on top of the development environment. Giving an AI assistant proper structured context about ABAP objects, instead of leaving it to infer from code completion, is a real improvement and the people doing it are doing it well.

We are not competing with that. We have a different goal, and one of our working principles is that we do not rebuild what the market already provides. Because everything here speaks MCP, those tools and ours can sit in the same landscape and serve the same consultant.

The difference is the audience. Tooling built on top of the development environment naturally serves the person who lives in the development environment. That improves the developer's part of the process. Our finding, after trying hard to improve exactly that part, is that the developer's part of the process was not the constraint.

The change we made

We built the toolchain for the consultant.

That is a different design problem. A consultant needs more than code generation. To take a requirement from a business user all the way to something testable, a consultant needs:

  • Knowledge of how this company has already built things, so the new thing is consistent with the old ones
  • Business data and transactions, so the result can be tested immediately against reality
  • Development tools, so the specification can become code
  • The company's own rules, so the code that comes out is the code this company would have written

Give a consultant those four things through an AI agent and something changes in the economics. The consultant does not translate the requirement to a developer. The consultant works the requirement into a functional specification, then a technical specification, then ABAP code, then tests it with real data, in one continuous session, while still holding the business context that made them the right person to understand it in the first place.

The magic is not the code generation. Code generation is a commodity. The magic is that a person who understands the requirement never has to hand it to someone who does not.

What the setup looks like

 Figure 1. The consultant works in one place. Four logical MCP servers supply knowledge, data, governance and tooling; the three platform-side ones can be deployed separately or combined. The interactive tier is exchangeable.

Four logical MCP servers, two backends, one place for the consultant to work. How they are deployed is a configuration choice, covered at the end of this section.

1. An MCP server published from the ABAP system itself

This is the piece that most differentiates the setup, so it is worth being precise about it.

The MCP server runs in the ABAP stack and is published through SICF. The reason is a different goal, not a different opinion about existing tooling. What this process needs from the ABAP system is business data, transactional actions and a handful of development tools, all provisioned under control. That is a provisioning problem, and the ABAP stack is where it gets solved.

None of that is a judgement about ADT. ADT is a development environment and it is very good at being one. This setup simply does not need that power to do its job, so we did not build toward it. If a customer wants it, the community MCP servers built on top of ADT connect alongside ours and serve the same consultant. We would far rather that happened than spend our time rebuilding something the market already provides and already does well.

Because it is published from the ABAP system, SAP's own authentication and authorization apply to every single call. There is no parallel permission model to maintain and no service user quietly holding more authority than the person using it. If a consultant is not authorized to see a plant, the agent does not see that plant either.

Provisioning is explicit and object by object. You nominate which tables, views and CDS views are exposed. You nominate which ABAP classes act as tools. There is a kill switch at the server.

Through it, the consultant's agent gets:

  • Business data: selected tables, views and CDS views
  • Business transactions: ABAP classes exposed as callable tools, so the agent can create and change documents the same way a user would
  • Development tools: read source code, read object metadata, read short dumps, inspect transports

That last group is what makes the specification honest. The agent does not recall what a table looks like. It reads it.

 Figure 2. The MCP server is a standard ICF service. Authentication and authorization are SAP's, not a parallel model.

 Figure 3. What the consultant actually sees: business transactions, nominated data sources and development tools in one list.

2. An MCP server for ABAP Code Intelligence

Most companies cannot answer a simple question about their own custom code: have we already built something like this?

Background AI agents on the Skybuffer AI platform read the entire custom estate out of the SAP backend and document it automatically. The documentation is vectorized immediately, which turns it into something the consultant's agent can search semantically during a task.

The effect is not mainly documentation for humans. It is that every new development starts with the question "what already exists here" answered. That raises integrity of the custom code base, drives reuse instead of reinvention, and surfaces harmonization and modernization candidates.

 Figure 4. Custom code is read, documented and vectorized continuously, so reuse is the default rather than an accident.

3. An MCP server for the company's development rules

Naming conventions. In-house ABAP standards. Clean ABAP. Clean core principles. Specification templates. The development contract that says what a functional specification must contain before it is allowed to become a technical specification.

These are usually in a wiki that nobody opens. Here they are in the task context, at the moment the decision is being made, which is the only moment they matter.

4. An MCP server for tooling

ABAP Cleaner and other post-processors, applied to generated code before a human looks at it.

This is deliberately an open ecosystem. SAP standard MCP servers, community ones, ADT-based servers for the developers who want them: they all connect alongside. Nothing here is exclusive, and nothing here duplicates something that already exists on the market.

A note on how these are deployed. The four above are a logical grouping rather than a required topology. The first is necessarily its own server, because it lives in the ABAP stack. The three provisioned from the Skybuffer AI platform can run as three servers or be combined into one, and which tools each exposes is configured per customer. We run ours combined, because our internal development process is a single process; a customer whose code standards and tooling sit with different owners may well want them apart. The configuration follows the customer's development process rather than the other way round.

 Figure 5. Platform-side tooling, here deployed as a single combined MCP server: search the documented estate, apply in-house rules, clean the generated code.

The orchestration layer

The MCP servers are the asset. The orchestration unit connects to them and can be exchanged. Which model sits there is a current engineering choice, and we cover the reasoning below.

Where the data lives, and who can support it

In serious conversations about this, two questions arrive before the technical ones. They deserve direct answers.

Your data stays yours, in your own infrastructure

The Skybuffer AI platform runs on SAP BTP or on SAP HANA on premise. Either way it is the customer's landscape. The documented custom code, the vector store built from it, the in-house rule base and the configuration of the development process all sit inside the customer's infrastructure and belong to the customer.

The MCP server that exposes business data runs inside the ABAP stack itself. Data is not copied out to a platform so that an agent can reach it. It is read in place, per call, under the requesting user's own SAP authorizations. Nothing is staged, replicated or synchronised into a third-party store to make any of this work.

This is a consequence of the architecture rather than a policy bolted on top of it. There is no separate data layer to govern, because there is no separate copy of the data.

Built on SAP technologies, so anyone who supports SAP can support this

The solution is developed using SAP technologies only. It is an ABAP add-on plus a BTP or HANA application. It is not a black box with a proprietary runtime or a specialist skill set attached to it.

That has a consequence people tend to underestimate at purchase time and feel sharply two years later: your own internal SAP team can support it, and so can any SAP partner you already work with. You are not introducing a component into your landscape that only one vendor is able to touch, and you are not making your ABAP estate dependent on a skill set your team does not have and cannot hire.

No lock-in to a closed architecture

Nothing here requires a particular cloud offering. The platform deploys where you already run SAP. The MCP layer is an open protocol, which is why customers can add SAP standard or community MCP servers next to ours, and why the orchestration unit can be exchanged without rebuilding anything underneath it.

The thing you are investing in is your own documented custom estate, your own rule base and your own provisioned tool set. Those stay yours regardless of what you decide to run on top of them.

Two model tiers, chosen for two different jobs

There is no single "the AI" in this architecture. There are two tiers doing unrelated work, and they are not staffed by the same model for good reasons.

The background tier runs on the customer's own model, usually self-hosted. The agents that read the entire custom code estate, document it and vectorize it are doing bulk work where latency is not a KPI anyone is optimizing. If a full pass takes a weekend, nothing is harmed. That makes them a natural fit for a self-hosted LLM inside the customer's landscape, which is what most customers choose. Some run them on a single small GPU unit; an NVIDIA DGX Spark class device is enough for this workload.

This tier matters most for the data question, because this is the tier that touches everything. Every custom object, every piece of business logic, the complete estate. That entire pass happens inside the customer's infrastructure, on a model the customer selected, and the resulting knowledge base stays there.

The interactive tier is where the consultant works, and today we run Opus 5 Max there. That choice is specific rather than incidental, and the reason is not "it writes nice code."

The constraint is discipline under a governed process. Our development contract requires the agent to read the framework contract from live implementations rather than recall it, to verify every table and field against the live dictionary, and to stop when something cannot be verified. A model that shortcuts tool calls to produce a faster, more complete-looking answer breaks that contract no matter how good the templates are.

So what we need from the interactive model is narrower than general capability. It has to keep calling tools, as many times as the task actually requires, until the context is genuinely complete. And it has to hold and reason over the very large runtime context that results from doing so. As of today, that combination is what Opus 5 Max does well, and it is why the generated ABAP comes out integrated with the existing custom development and accurate to the customer's backend release rather than to a plausible average of the internet.

One honest boundary

The interactive tier is the single component that can sit outside the landscape. What crosses is the context assembled for one task, not the estate. We would rather state that plainly than let a reader discover it.

The architecture is built so that this position is exchangeable, which is the practical answer for anyone whose isolation requirements are absolute: point the interactive tier at a self-hosted model as well. Nothing underneath changes, because the MCP servers, the knowledge base and the governance do not care what is connected to them. The honest trade-off is that today you will give up some code quality by doing so, and how much depends on how well the model you choose sustains long tool-calling chains.

Why this does not just produce confident nonsense

This is the first question every experienced SAP person asks, and they are right to ask it.

The answer is not "the model is good." The answer is that the process forbids guessing, and the tooling makes not guessing cheaper than guessing.

A worked example from our own governed pipeline. The agent was building a new MCP tool and needed the framework contract: superclass, method signatures, error mechanism. The rule in our development contract is that it must read this from existing implementations, never recall it. So it read five objects in a fixed order.

Two things came out of that which no amount of model quality would have produced:

First, the metadata-reading tool reports a blank superclass for classes that genuinely do inherit. Reading the source instead showed the real inheritance. An agent working from metadata alone would have generated a structurally wrong class that implemented interfaces directly instead of inheriting from the framework base. It would have looked plausible and failed on activation.

Second, and more instructive: the specification needed two SAP authorization objects. The agent could not verify them. The system exposes no metadata path for authorization objects, and no existing tool in our library performed a comparable check that could be read as precedent. A generative tool optimizing for a complete-looking answer would have filled in the two most likely names.

It did not. It recorded them as unverified, raised a blocking open question with a named owner, isolated the two values in the code as single-point-of-change constants, and stated that the object must not be transported beyond development until a human confirms them.

That is the difference between a demo and a development process. The valuable output is not only the code. It is the code plus an explicit, honest list of what is still unknown.

What a task actually looks like

  1. The consultant brings a business requirement, usually straight from the conversation with the user.
  2. The agent loads the governed context: templates, in-house rules, and a semantic search of what already exists in the custom estate.
  3. Together they produce a functional specification. The agent verifies every table and field it names against the live system as it writes.
  4. The functional specification becomes a technical specification, with the framework contract read from real implementations rather than recalled.
  5. Code is generated from the technical specification, then run through ABAP Cleaner.
  6. The consultant tests it immediately, using the business transactions and data exposed through the same MCP server, without leaving the session or booking anyone's time.
  7. Unknowns that could not be resolved are listed as open questions with owners. Blocking ones stop the object from moving forward.

Steps 3 through 6 used to be a multi-week loop involving at least two people and several meetings.

What we measured

Inside our own company, within the first weeks:

  • About 40% reduction in the ABAP development capacity we needed. This is not a ceiling. We are still optimizing.
  • For the first time ever, not enough tasks to fill the ABAP developer queue — an inversion of the constraint we had been fighting for years.
  • Consultants completing volumes of work in one to two weeks that previously took far longer.

With a customer already running the new process, the effect showed up almost immediately. These are results from the first weeks of adoption, not from a mature steady state:

  • A backlog of critical business requirements cleared, after sitting unaddressed
  • Most projects delivered to UAT within one month
  • Up to 90% savings per project
  • $0.1M–$0.2M USD returned each week

The number the customer cared about most was none of those. It was that the queue of business requirements shrank. Business users stopped hearing "that is in the backlog" as the standard answer to a reasonable request.

That speed of return is the part worth pausing on. This is not a transformation programme that pays back over two years. The mechanism is simply that work stops waiting in a handoff, so the effect appears as soon as the first requirements go through the new path.

Set against the roughly 10% cost saving that classic developer-focused automation typically delivers, the difference is not incremental. It comes from moving the work, not from speeding up the typing.

The honest part

A few things we would want to know if we were reading this rather than writing it.

The consultant's job gets harder, not easier. This surprised us. Consultants were exhausted by the old cycle of meetings, explanation, testing and re-explanation, and they were glad to see it go. But spending the day in dialogue with a very knowledgeable agent is intense work. It demands more decisions per hour than the old process did. Our consultants report being happier, and they also report being more tired. Plan for that.

You still need ABAP developers. Complex architecture, performance work at scale, framework-level changes, and review of anything sensitive still need senior ABAP judgement. What changes is the ratio, and what those developers spend their day on. We reduced capacity by 40%; we did not reduce it to zero, and we would not want to.

This requires governance to exist before it can be automated. If your naming conventions, development standards and specification templates are informal or absent, the agent has nothing to be grounded in and you will get plausible, inconsistent output. The uncomfortable prerequisite is writing your rules down.

The first weeks are not representative. Early gains come partly from clearing a backlog that had accumulated. The steady-state number is lower than the first-month number. We are still measuring ours.

Where to start

You do not have to do all of this at once, and you should not.

  1. Make your custom estate legible. Run automated documentation over existing custom code and vectorize it. This has standalone value even if you stop here, because it answers "what do we already have" for every future project.
  2. Publish a narrow MCP server from your ABAP system. Start read-only, with a small set of nominated tables and development tools. SAP authorization does the access control, so the blast radius is whatever you provision.
  3. Write down the rules. Naming conventions, in-house standards, and one governed specification template. Put them where the agent reads them.
  4. Pick one consultant and one real requirement. Not a pilot with a toy scope. A real thing somebody is waiting for.
  5. Add transactional tools only once reading is solid, so the consultant can test in the same session.

Closing

We spent a long time, and a great deal of effort, trying to make developers faster before we accepted that we were optimizing the wrong side of the handoff. That conclusion was harder to reach than it looks written down, and we would not have believed it without running it on ourselves first.

The result is not that ABAP developers are unnecessary. It is that a large share of custom development does not need to cross the boundary between the person who understands the requirement and the person who implements it. When it does not have to cross, it does not have to wait.

If your business users are being told their requirements are in the queue, the queue is probably not a capacity problem. It is probably a translation problem.

The Skybuffer AI platform runs on SAP BTP or on SAP HANA on premise, inside the customer's own landscape, and is built entirely on SAP technologies, so an internal SAP team or any SAP partner can support it. It is available on SAP Store. It was SAP Certified as Built with SAP Business AI, and was a finalist in the SAP Innovation Awards 2025 as a partner-built product. If you are working on the same problem from the developer side, we would like to compare notes, and we are genuinely interested in where this approach breaks.

entry.title: Troubleshooting a Hubwoo Loading Issue from SAP GUI After a Microsoft Edge Browser Update
entry.content:
Troubleshooting a Hubwoo Loading Issue from SAP GUI After a Microsoft Edge Browser Update

Introduction

In SAP Basis support, we often troubleshoot issues that initially appear to be SAP application problems but are actually related to the user's local client environment.

I recently encountered one such issue where Hubwoo was not opening correctly from SAP GUI. Instead of displaying the expected Hubwoo application, the screen remained in a continuous loading state.

What made the issue interesting was the timing: the problem was observed after a Microsoft Edge browser version update.

Initially, the symptom could have led us toward several areas—SAP backend connectivity, network communication, certificates, or the external application itself. However, based on the behavior and the timing of the issue, I also considered the SAP GUI browser-control layer.

The eventual resolution was simple:

SAP GUI Settings → Local Data → File Lifetime → Clear Browser Control Cache → Restart SAP GUI

After performing this, Hubwoo opened successfully.

In this blog, I will share the troubleshooting approach, the reasoning behind checking the client-side browser cache, the resolution, and the lessons I took from the incident.

What is Hubwoo?

Hubwoo is an enterprise e-procurement platform used for procurement and supplier-related processes.

In an SAP environment, external procurement applications such as Hubwoo may be accessed through SAP GUI or through an integration flow involving SAP and external services.

From a troubleshooting perspective, this means that an issue reported as:

"Hubwoo is not opening from SAP"

does not necessarily mean that there is a problem with the SAP application server.

Depending on the implementation, the access path may involve multiple components:

Therefore, it is important to troubleshoot the complete path instead of focusing only on the SAP backend.

The Incident

What happened?

A user reported that Hubwoo could not be opened successfully from SAP GUI.

When Hubwoo was launched:

  • The page started loading.

  • The loading did not complete.

  • The expected Hubwoo application interface was not displayed.

  • The issue was observed after a Microsoft Edge browser version update.

From the user's perspective, it looked like an application availability issue.

However, the SAP system itself was not showing an obvious indication that the backend was unavailable.

My Initial Troubleshooting Approach

This was the part of the incident that I found particularly useful from a Basis troubleshooting perspective.

When an external application does not open from SAP GUI, there are several possible areas to investigate:

  • SAP application server

  • SAP GUI

  • Browser control

  • Network connectivity

  • DNS

  • Firewall

  • SSL/TLS communication

  • External application availability

  • Local cache or session data

Instead of immediately making changes on the SAP backend, I first looked at the timeline and behavior of the issue.

The important clue was that the issue appeared after a Microsoft Edge browser version update.

The Hubwoo page was not completely unavailable—it was reaching the loading stage and then remaining there.

This made the client-side browser-control environment a reasonable area to investigate.

Why I Looked at the SAP GUI Browser Control

One lesson I have learned from SAP Basis troubleshooting is that the component closest to the symptom is not always the SAP application server.

Since the issue occurred while launching a browser-based external application through SAP GUI, I considered whether locally stored browser-control data could be contributing to the loading behaviour.

This was also a relatively low-risk troubleshooting step compared with making changes to the SAP backend, network configuration, certificates, or other productive components.

Resolution

The issue was resolved by clearing the Browser Control Cache in SAP GUI.

Step 1 – Open SAP GUI Settings

Open SAP GUI and access the SAP GUI settings/options.

Step 2 – Navigate to Local Data

Go to:

Local Data

Step 3 – Open File Lifetime

Under Local Data, open:

File Lifetime

Step 4 – Clear Browser Control Cache

Select:

Clear Browser Control Cache

This clears the locally stored browser-control cache maintained within the SAP GUI environment.

Step 5 – Restart SAP GUI

After clearing the cache:

  1. Close SAP GUI.

  2. Restart SAP GUI.

  3. Try opening Hubwoo.

Step 6 – Verify the Application

After restarting SAP GUI, Hubwoo was launched again.

The application loaded successfully instead of remaining on the continuous loading screen.

This confirmed that clearing the Browser Control Cache had resolved the issue in this particular incident.


Resolution Flow


 

Before and After

Before

The application remained stuck in the loading state.

After

After clearing the Browser Control Cache and restarting SAP GUI, Hubwoo opened normally.

Why Can Clearing the Browser Control Cache Help?

Browser-based applications depend on locally stored information, including cached resources and browser-control data.

When the browser environment or related components are updated, existing cached information can sometimes contribute to unexpected application behavior.

In this incident, clearing the Browser Control Cache restored the expected behavior.

However, I would avoid describing this as a definitive technical root cause because the incident did not include a detailed comparison of browser-control versions or a confirmed SAP Note/root-cause analysis.

The conclusion I can confidently make is:

The issue was observed after a Microsoft Edge browser update, and clearing the SAP GUI Browser Control Cache resolved the Hubwoo loading problem.

What I Learned From This Incident

1. Don't assume every SAP GUI issue is an SAP backend issue

This incident reminded me that when a user says:

"The application is not opening from SAP."

the troubleshooting should not automatically start with the SAP application server.

2. The incident timeline can provide valuable clues

The fact that the issue appeared after a browser update was an important clue.

A recent client-side change should always be considered when an application that was previously working suddenly starts behaving differently.

This does not prove that the update caused the issue, but it helps narrow the troubleshooting area.

3. Start with low-risk troubleshooting

Before making changes to a productive SAP system, it is worth checking whether the problem can be isolated to the client environment.

In this case, clearing the Browser Control Cache was:

  • Simple

  • Low risk

  • Quick to perform

  • Easy to validate

Most importantly, it solved the issue without requiring a backend change.

4. Don't overstate the root cause

One of the biggest takeaways for me was the difference between observing a correlation and proving a root cause.

The timeline was:

Microsoft Edge update → Hubwoo loading issue → Browser Control Cache cleared → Hubwoo works

This establishes a strong troubleshooting correlation, but it does not by itself prove exactly what changed internally.

For incident documentation and knowledge-sharing articles, I believe it is better to clearly separate:

What we observed from What we conclusively proved.

Practical Troubleshooting Decision Tree

When an external application such as Hubwoo remains stuck while loading from SAP GUI, I would approach it like this:

 

Incident Summary

ItemDetails
ApplicationHubwoo
Access MethodSAP GUI
SymptomHubwoo continuously loading
Observed TimelineAfter a Microsoft Edge browser version update
Initial FocusSAP GUI / Browser Control layer
ResolutionClear Browser Control Cache
NavigationLocal Data → File Lifetime
Post-Resolution ActionRestart SAP GUI
ResultHubwoo opened successfully
Backend ChangeNo backend change was required for the reported resolution

Key Takeaways

🔹Look beyond the SAP backend

When SAP GUI is used to access an external application, the issue may exist in the local SAP GUI or browser-control layer.

🔹Use the timeline as a troubleshooting clue

A recent browser or client update can help narrow down the investigation.

🔹Try simple, low-risk checks first

Clearing the Browser Control Cache was enough to resolve this particular incident.

🔹Distinguish correlation from root cause

An issue occurring after a browser update does not automatically mean that the browser update is the confirmed root cause.

🔹Document what actually worked

Even a simple resolution can be valuable to other Basis administrators when it is documented with the exact navigation and verification steps.

Final Verification and Conclusion

After clearing the Browser Control Cache and restarting SAP GUI, I opened Hubwoo again and verified that the application loaded successfully instead of remaining on the continuous loading screen.

For me, the main takeaway from this incident was that SAP Basis troubleshooting should consider the complete user-to-application path. An issue that appears to be an SAP or external-application problem may sometimes be resolved at the SAP GUI client layer.

The final resolution in this incident was:

SAP GUI Settings → Local Data → File Lifetime → Clear Browser Control Cache → Restart SAP GUI → Open Hubwoo

Although the issue was observed after a Microsoft Edge browser update, the exact technical root cause was not conclusively established. What was confirmed through troubleshooting was that clearing the Browser Control Cache restored normal Hubwoo access.

Hopefully, this experience can help other SAP Basis and support teams quickly check the SAP GUI browser-control layer when they encounter a similar "application continuously loading" symptom.

entry.title: Ewelina Siudzińska
entry.content:
More about Ewelina Siudzińska in SAP Community


First Name, Last Name: Ewelina Siudzińska
Location (City, Country): Katowice, Poland
Occupation: SAP Consultant (BW & BI)

 

 


Ewelina, tell us about yourself.
Who are you, what do you like to do, what is important to you?

My family says I am hard-working and determined. My friends say I am well-organized and reliable. I think I am just authentic and myself. Most the time, I go against the flow! I do not listen to music that everyone else listens to, and I do not spend my holidays on a sunbed with an all-inclusive package. Instead, I choose  conscious travelling with every hour of sightseeing planned out 😉 and as much physical activity as possible. I try to keep a good work-life balance. My work and personal development are very important to me, and I spend a lot of time working towards my goals. But living my own life is also important to me. Sports such as fitness, cycling, walking, and swimming help me achieve this on an ordinary day. I enjoy reading crime novels, and when I do not have time for that, I listen to audiobooks while doing other daily activities. I love cooking and enjoy trying new flavors during my travels.


What is your area of expertise?
What does a usual day at work look like for you?

I work as SAP BI and BW consultant. I specialize in designing and implementing operational and strategic reports. These are primarily activities aimed at working closely with functional teams to understand reporting needs and deliver solutions that meet business objectives. The icing on the cake is the creation of interactive dashboards in SAC based on models I built in SAP BW. I collaborate on system upgrades, enhancements, and migrations. My tasks also entail maintaining extractors from SAP ERP, but also deploying standard and custom extractors from the S/4HANA system. This involves collaborating with teams responsible for handling subscribers’ queues.


What inspired you to become an SAP Champion in SAP Community?

Since 2019, I have been building the SAP Community in Silesia, in Katowice. I invested a significant amount of my personal time in this, but it was worth it! Currently, our Katowice Community: https://community.sap.com/t5/katowice/gh-p/katowice is a strong group of specialists who enjoy each other's company. It has always been my idea to surround myself with SAP experts and feel even more motivated to act in my region. That is why becoming an SAP Champion was a natural next step. I am grateful for being nominated to the Community of SAP Champions. I would like to get to know all of you and, in time, be able to say: “Yes, I know this person, he/she is a specialist in ... with whom I had the opportunity to talk/work together on organizing an event / etc.”


How do you learn in SAP Community?
What is your daily/weekly routine in SAP Community?

When I am looking for an idea to solve a problem, I always browse https://community.sap.com/ to see if anyone else has done something similar. I often find inspiration there, and sometimes it opens my mind to a different solution than I had planned.

Besides, I believe that the best way to learn from the SAP Community is through conversation. That is why I am initiating meetings in the region to enable people with different experiences in SAP to meet and talk. It always broadens horizons and often allows everyone to learn from others.


What is your suggestion to get the most out of SAP Community?

The SAP Community is made up of wonderful people. It would be great to have the opportunity to meet in person, especially those who are heavily involved in the Community. I think that at least once a year, SAP should organize and sponsor such a meeting for SAP Champions and Mentors. This would give us the opportunity to get to know each other, exchange experiences, expand our cooperation and much more.

My second suggestion is to develop a prestigious program for speakers at events, which would give them greater recognition and benefits. As an organizer of SAP meetups and meetings, I encounter obstacles in finding speakers for the events I have organized and plan to organize in the future. It is not that there are not any specialists! There are many specialists in the region, but few people are willing to volunteer their time to prepare presentations and lectures. This can be easily changed by following the example of other companies that have a strong community around their product, such as Microsoft. Or create your own program in which SAP would reward the commitment of speakers.

Ewelina's question to you:
What do you think about my suggestions above to get the most out of SAP Community?
Feel free to write whether you agree with those and share your opinion.

entry.title: Migrating SAP PowerDesigner Object Codes to erwin Data Modeler
entry.content:
Introduction

Migrating a data model between different modeling tools is not only about transferring entities, attributes, and relationships. Preserving source-model traceability can be equally important.

During a migration from SAP PowerDesigner to erwin Data Modeler, the original object codes defined in the source model may need to remain available after migration. Depending on the model type, these codes may originate from a Physical Data Model (PDM), Logical Data Model (LDM), or Conceptual Data Model (CDM).

This blog presents a Python-based approach to extract object codes from a PowerDesigner model and associate them with the corresponding objects in an erwin XML export.

The source object code is stored in the erwin object's Notes as a structured provenance entry:

[Object_code] SMPL_ACQSTN

The important point is that this does not replace existing information in erwin. The code is added as a separate note event, allowing previously migrated comments or notes to remain intact.

1. Migration Approach

The overall process is:

PowerDesigner Model
(PDM / LDM / CDM)
        │
        ▼
Extract Object Codes
        │
        ▼
Match with erwin Objects
        │
        ▼
Add Object Code to erwin Notes
        │
        ▼
Preprocessed erwin XML

The approach can be applied to different PowerDesigner model objects depending on the migration scenario. The generated note follows a simple convention:

[Object_code] <PowerDesigner Object Code>

For example:
[Object_code] SMPL_ACQSTN

This prefix makes the generated provenance information distinguishable from normal documentation or comments.

2. The Traceability Problem

Consider a PowerDesigner object with:

Name: Sample Acquisition
Code: SMPL_ACQSTN

After migration, the corresponding erwin object may contain the name and physical name, but the original PowerDesigner object code may no longer be readily available.

This creates a traceability challenge.

After migration, we may want to answer questions such as:

  • What was the original PowerDesigner object code?
  • Which source object corresponds to this erwin object?
  • Can the migrated object be traced back to the source model?
  • Can the source code be retained without modifying existing documentation?

Instead of introducing a completely separate mapping repository, the approach stores the source object code directly in the corresponding erwin object's Notes.

3. Source-to-Target Concept

The basic concept is:

PowerDesigner Object
        │
        │ Object Code
        ▼
erwin Object Note

For example: 

PowerDesigner
Name: Sample Acquisition
Code: SMPL_ACQSTN

        ↓

erwin Notes
[Object_code] SMPL_ACQSTN

The same concept can be applied to objects originating from a PDM, LDM, or CDM, provided the corresponding source and target objects can be identified.

4. Why Use erwin Notes?

One option would be to modify an existing erwin property to hold the source object code.

However, this can introduce several problems:

  • an existing value could be overwritten;
  • information already migrated from PowerDesigner could be lost;
  • the target model's original information could be altered;
  • repeated migration runs could become difficult to control.

The Notes structure provides a convenient location for maintaining this additional provenance information.

The solution therefore treats the object code as a provenance event, rather than as a replacement for an existing property.

For example: 

Note #1
[Existing migrated comment]

Note #2
[Object_code] SMPL_ACQSTN

If another migration step has already created several notes, the object code becomes the next note instead of replacing them.

5. Understanding the erwin Note Structure

The erwin XML export represents notes using a structure similar to:

<Note_List_Array>
    <Note_List HandleNonPrintableChar="Y" index="0">
        ...
    </Note_List>
</Note_List_Array>

The Note List is associated with the relevant EntityProps or AttributeProps  section.

When a Note List does not already exist, the implementation inserts the required structure at the appropriate location.

Each note record follows the internal structure expected by the erwin export format. The generated note therefore needs to follow this structure rather than simply inserting arbitrary XML text.

6. Matching PowerDesigner Objects with erwin

Once the source object codes are extracted, the utility identifies the corresponding erwin objects using a three-level matching strategy. 

Level 1 — Name + Code
PowerDesigner Name  = erwin Name
PowerDesigner Code  = erwin Physical Name

Level 2 — Code
PowerDesigner Code = erwin Physical Name

Level 3 — Name
PowerDesigner Name = erwin Name

The comparison is performed case-insensitively.

Fallback matching is accepted only when the candidate is unique, reducing the risk of assigning an object code to the wrong target object.

7. Why Byte-Level XML Modification?

Instead of reading and rewriting the entire erwin XML through a conventional DOM writer, the implementation uses the XML parser to locate the required objects and byte positions.

The new Note structures are then inserted directly into the original XML byte stream.

This helps avoid unintended changes such as:

  • line-ending normalization;
  • conversion of <X></X> into <X/>;
  • namespace declaration reordering;
  • other formatting changes introduced by XML serializers.

As a result, only the required portions of the original erwin XML are modified.

8. GitHub Repository

The complete implementation, usage instructions, and supporting files are available in the repository below.
GitHub Repository : GitHub - Writzzzz/Object_Code_Migration--SAP_PD_to_ERWIN · GitHub

The repository can be used as a reference for implementing or adapting the object-code migration approach for different PowerDesigner-to-erwin migration scenarios.

Conclusion

Preserving source metadata is an important aspect of data-model migration, particularly when the migrated model needs to remain traceable to its original source.

This approach extracts PowerDesigner object codes, identifies the corresponding erwin objects, and stores the codes as structured Notes.

By generalizing the approach across PDM, LDM, and CDM, the same mechanism can be used to retain source-object provenance across different PowerDesigner model types.

Key Benefits

  • Preserves original PowerDesigner object codes
  • Maintains source-to-target traceability
  • Preserves existing erwin Notes
  • Can be applied across PDM, LDM, and CDM scenarios
  • Supports object-level matching and reporting
  • Minimizes unnecessary changes to the original erwin XML

entry.title: Kit-to-Stock in SAP EWM with SAP PP Integration Configuration and End-to-End Process
entry.content:
Abstract

Kit-to-Stock is an SAP Extended Warehouse Management (SAP EWM) process in which multiple component products are picked and assembled into a finished kit. The completed kit is received into warehouse stock and remains available for future sales orders or other business requirements. This process allows organizations to prepare frequently requested kits in advance, improving product availability and warehouse efficiency.

Introduction

In the Kit-to-Stock process, kits are created based on anticipated demand rather than for a specific customer order. The warehouse picks the required components, transfers them to a Value-Added Services (VAS) work center, performs the kitting activity, consumes the components, posts the completed kit and places it into storage.

In a decentralized SAP EWM scenario, the process can be initiated through an SAP ERP or SAP ECC production order. When the production order is released, an outbound delivery is created for the kit components, and an inbound delivery is created for the finished kit. These delivery documents are distributed to SAP EWM for warehouse execution.

The main benefits of Kit-to-Stock include:

  • Faster customer-order fulfillment
  • Reduced picking and packing time during order processing
  • Better control and visibility of component consumption
  • Improved availability of finished-kit inventory
  • Standardized kitting activities at the VAS work center
  • Integration between production-order processing and warehouse execution

Kit-to-Stock Process Flow

The following process flow illustrates how an SAP ECC production order initiates component staging and finished-kit receipt activities in decentralized SAP EWM.

Configuration

The following configuration is based on a decentralized SAP EWM system integrated with an SAP ECC system.

#1 Define order type(ECC)

SPRO->Production->Shop Floor control ->Master data ->Order->Define order types

A dedicated production order type, KTS1 – KIT TO STOCK, is configured for the Kit-to-Stock process. The order category is maintained as 10 (Production Order), which allows the order to use standard SAP production-order functionality.

The PP01 settlement profile is assigned for production-order cost settlement, while the CO partner update is maintained as Semi-active. Residence times are also defined to control how long completed orders remain in the system before they become eligible for archiving.        

#2 Production Scheduling profile(ECC)

SPRO->Production->Shop Floor control ->Master data ->Define Production Scheduling profile

The production scheduling profile KTS1 – KIT TO STOCK is maintained for plant XXXX. In the Transport section, the Kit to Stock in EWM indicator is selected, and production order type KTS1 is assigned under Make-to-Stock Production.

This indicator controls the integration between the production order and SAP EWM. When the production order is released, the system creates:

  • An outbound delivery for supplying and consuming the kit components.
  • An inbound delivery for receiving the completed kit header.

Both deliveries are then distributed to EWM for component picking, kit creation, goods receipt, and final put-away.

#3 Define relevance for VAS(EWM)

SPRO->SCM EWM->EWM->Cross process Settings ->VAS->Define relevance for VAS

This configuration connects the Kit-to-Stock VAS order with the corresponding EWM delivery documents for warehouse 1XXX. VAS order type KTS is assigned to order category D – VAS for Creating Kits for Stock.

For component processing, the system uses outbound document type OKTS with item type OKSR. For receiving the completed kit header, it uses inbound document type IKTS with item type IKSR. Stock type F2 is assigned to both document flows, and VAS procedure 0VSK controls the value-added service activities required for kit creation.

These settings allow EWM to create and process:

  • An outbound delivery order for picking and consuming the kit components.
  • An inbound delivery for receiving and putting away the completed kit.

#4 Document types for VAS for Kit to Stock(EWM)

SPRO->SCM EWM->EWM->Cross process Settings ->VAS->Document types for VAS for Kit to Stock

In this configuration, VAS order type KTS is assigned to order category D – VAS for Creating Kits for Stock for the applicable warehouse.

The following document and item types control the delivery flow:

  • OKTS / OKSR: Outbound delivery document and item types used for picking and consuming the kit components.
  • IKTS / IKSR: Inbound delivery document and item types used for receiving and putting away the completed kit header.
  • F2: Stock type assigned to both the outbound and inbound processes.
  • 0VSK: VAS procedure that controls the activities required to create the kit.

This configuration enables EWM to connect the component outbound process with the finished-kit inbound process under the same Kit-to-Stock VAS order.

#5 Map Document types from ERP system to EWM(EWM)

SPRO->SCM EWM->EWM->Interfaces->ERP Integration->Delivery processing -> Map Document types from ERP system to EWM

This configuration maps the delivery types received from the connected ERP business system to the corresponding EWM document types.

For the Kit-to-Stock process:

  • ERP inbound delivery type HID is mapped to EWM inbound document type IKTS.
  • ERP outbound delivery type HOD is mapped to EWM outbound document type OKTS.

Conclusion

Kit-to-Stock integrates SAP PP and SAP EWM to support the advance assembly of component materials into a finished kit. When the production order is released in ECC, the system creates an outbound delivery for the kit components and an inbound delivery for the finished kit. These documents are transferred to EWM, where the warehouse performs component picking, consumption posting, kit creation, goods receipt, and final put away.

The process provides clear visibility across the complete document flow, from the production order in ECC to warehouse execution in EWM. With the correct production scheduling profile, VAS settings, document-type mapping, item-type mapping, and warehouse-process configuration, organizations can prepare frequently required kits in advance and reduce processing time during customer-order fulfilment.
