entry.title: Vehicle-to-Grid integration in IS-U Billing
entry.content:
The Utilities industry is facing an increasing demand for flexible solutions to manage Distributed Energy Resources (DER), driven by the growing adoption of new technologies and commercial offerings for energy consumers. One such scenario is Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G), which is transforming electric vehicles from energy consumers into flexible energy resources. Besides charging and discharging electricity, several utilities and mobility providers are beginning to remunerate customers for keeping their vehicle connected to the grid and available for flexibility services.

Inspired by Holger Schweinfurth's Vehicle-to-Grid demonstration, I explored how such a scenario could be implemented using only standard SAP IS-U configuration. This led me to build and test two different scenarios in our SAP S/4HANA system:

Besides energy measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh), the V2G model may introduce a second commercial dimension: the time during which a vehicle remains connected and available for grid services. While this duration may be recorded in minutes, a commercial model may remunerate this availability using an hourly rate.

In this blog series, we will look at the customizing requirements needed not only to capture Meter Reading (MR) results recorded in kilowatt-hours (kWh), but also to capture the time a vehicle remains connected to the grid in minutes (MIN) and subsequently use this information for billing.

This reflects an emerging commercial model in which customers may receive an availability payment for keeping a compatible EV connected and available for grid services.

It is important to bear in mind that this blog series does not describe a complete V2G solution or the technical integration between an EV, charging infrastructure, energy management system and utility backend. Instead, it focuses specifically on how standard SAP IS-U device and billing configuration can be used to model and bill selected V2G-related quantities.

Furthermore, we will also have a closer look on how IS-U rates can be configured to allow the billing and invoicing of MR Results registered in both kWh and MIN.

As a final addition to this blog series, there will be a final part on how the Convergent Invoicing (CI) component of Billing and Revenue Innovation Management (BRIM) could be leveraged to calculate an availability bonus for a customer without directly maintaining the entire V2G set-up in IS-U.

By the end of this blog series, you will have an end-to-end example showing how standard SAP IS-U can bill:

  • energy imported from the grid (kWh),
  • energy exported back to the grid (kWh), and
  • availability time, measured in minutes and remunerated in hours,

using only standard SAP IS-U configuration and billing functionality. To top it all off, you will also have seen a possible strategy through which the availability bonus could be applied by integrating CI in IS-U billing.

 

Part 1: Business context and device/register configuration

 

This first part of this series will be dedicated to the set-up of two IS-U Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) installations. In this example, the V2G scenario is represented through three commercially relevant quantities: energy consumed while charging, energy exported while discharging, and the time during which the vehicle remains connected and available for grid services. To represent these requirements, two scenarios were built in our SAP S/4HANA system.

The first scenario uses a single device with three registers. Two registers measure the energy consumed during charging and exported during discharging in kWh, while the third register measures the time the vehicle remains connected to the grid in minutes (MIN). The second scenario uses two separate devices: one for the energy quantities measured in kWh and another for the connection time measured in MIN.

The image of the data environment below gives an overview of the set-up in our SAP S/4HANA system.

Assuming your SAP system already has an adequate material (MM) configured to allow the creation of electricity meters in SAP IS-U, a new register group will have to be configured to capture the MR results both KWH and MIN.

This can be achieved by simply using transaction EG04 or by navigating through the SAP MENU as illustrated below:

SAP MENU >> Device Management >> Technology >> Register Group >> EG04: Create

In this example Register Group E_V2G was created to meet the business requirement for the first scenario. Two registers measuring the consumption in KWH and a third one measuring the time connected to the grid in MIN:

For the second scenario, which uses two separate devices, the E_V2G register group was used as a template to create two dedicated register groups

    1. E_V2GC – Register group for device exclusively measuring in kWh

    2. E_V2GT – Register group for device exclusively measuring in MIN

Since MIN is not the typical unit used for an electricity register, an additional configuration step is required before it can be assigned to the register category. The relevant division and register categories must be linked to the dimension containing the UoM MIN.

Register group E_V2G – Register categories.

This can be achieved using the following customizing path:

SAP Customizing Implementation Guide >> SAP Utilities >> Device Management >> Technology >> Register Group >> Allocate Units of Measurement to Register Categories

Table T006 allows you to easily verify to which dimension(s) the required UoM(s) belong(s):

Link between UoM and Dimension in table T006.

This can also be verified by navigating through the following customizing path:

SAP Customizing Implementation Guide >> ABAP Platform >> General Settings >> Check Units of Measurement

Once the register group has been configured in line with the business requirement, the devices can be created with the newly created register groups:

ISU-EWALLBOX with register group E_V2G.

ISU-WALLBOX with register group E_V2GC.

1 with register group E_V2GT.

The next step would be to first technically install the devices and then realize the billing relevant installation in the IS-U installation provided for this use case.

Scenario 1:

Device ISU-EWALLBOX installed in installation 4100000512.

Rate data of installation 4100000512.

Scenario 2:

Device ISU-WALLBOX in conjunction with device 1 installed in installation 4100000513.

Rate data of installation 4100000513.

Before the billing-relevant installation of the device can be realized, the IS-U rates required to register the consumptions must already be configured for the installations concerned. In addition, the rate determination linking the rate category to the active rates through a rate type will also be required. These topics will be covered in the next part of this blogging series, where we will take a closer look at the rate and operand configuration and explore some of the more interesting aspects of the V2G billing scenario.

Over the next few weeks, the following blog posts will be published:

Part 2: From Meter Reading Results to Billable Quantities

Part 3: From Measured Quantities to Billing and Invoicing

Part 4: Leveraging Convergent Invoicing (CI) for calculation of availability bonus

entry.title: Inbound IDoc Custom Fields Converted to Uppercase Despite Lowercase Configuration
entry.content:
We enhanced a standard inbound IDoc with custom header and item fields. During inbound processing, lowercase values received in the IDoc are being converted to uppercase before updating the application tables. One field uses CHAR20 without a domain, while another uses a lowercase-enabled domain. Looking for guidance on whether this is standard SAP behavior, a data element/domain issue, or a product limitation.

Body

Background

We recently enhanced a standard Inbound IDoc by introducing custom fields at both header and item levels.

Header Field

  • Segment Field: E1EDK01-ZZAAS_INDICATOR
  • Data Element: Based on predefined type CHAR20
  • No custom domain assigned

Item Field

  • Segment Field: E1EDP01-ORD_ITEM_06-ZZOFFER_TYPE
  • Data Element uses a custom domain
  • Domain is configured with Lowercase Allowed

Our business requirement is to preserve the exact case of the values received in the inbound IDoc.

Observed Behavior

The inbound IDoc contains lowercase values, but during processing the values are converted to uppercase before being saved to the application tables.

Values Received in IDoc

 
E1EDK01-ZZAAS_INDICATOR = aas indicator
 
E1EDP01-ORD_ITEM_06-ZZOFFER_TYPE = pct1
 
Values Stored After Inbound Processing
 
 
E1EDK01-ZZAAS_INDICATOR = AAS INDICATOR
 
E1EDP01-ORD_ITEM_06-ZZOFFER_TYPE = PCT1
 
This behavior is observed even for the field whose domain has the Lowercase indicator enabled.

Analysis Performed

  • Verified that the custom domain for ZZOFFER_TYPE has the Lowercase checkbox enabled.
  • Confirmed that no conversion exit is assigned to the domain.
  • Verified that the inbound IDoc payload contains the values in lowercase.
  • Observed that the values are converted to uppercase during inbound processing before being persisted.

Questions for the Community

  1. Is there any standard SAP inbound IDoc processing logic that automatically converts custom character fields to uppercase?
  2. Should the Lowercase Allowed setting on the domain be sufficient to preserve the case during inbound processing?
  3. Does using a predefined CHAR20 data element without a dedicated domain cause SAP to force uppercase values?

entry.title: I tried the SAC Lite Viewer — and my story didn't even qualify
entry.content:
In the comments on my last performance write-up, a fellow member made a valuable point: before optimizing render times widget by widget, try the Lite Viewer. It decouples the viewer from the designer persona and can significantly cut the client-side load — targeting exactly the frontend cost I had been measuring, not the backend.

I promised a follow-up. Here it is — and it didn't go the way I expected, which is precisely why it's worth sharing.

What I expected vs. what happened

My plan was simple: open my story in view mode, confirm it ran through the Lite Viewer, and compare the render behavior against my earlier numbers.

The catch: the Lite Viewer is not a button you press. SAP Analytics Cloud switches to it automatically when a story is eligible — and silently falls back to the full Optimized (Unified) experience when it isn't. No error, no warning. So "run the Lite Viewer" really means "make the story eligible, open it, and then verify which viewer actually served it."

To verify, I didn't rely on feel. I checked the tenant telemetry in System Overview, under Opened Stories per Story Version:

  • Light Weight Viewer: — (no opens)
  • Unified Story: 1 (my open landed here)

The verdict is unambiguous: my story did not go through the Lite Viewer. It fell back to the full Unified Story experience.

Why it didn't qualify

The reason is the one hinted at in that comment thread. My story sits on a Planning model. As soon as SAP Analytics Cloud sees a Planning context, it routes the story to the Unified Story experience rather than the Lite Viewer. Planning-capable content and the Lite Viewer don't mix — the viewer is designed for lightweight, view-only consumption.

So the render savings I was hoping to measure were never on the table for this story. Not because the Lite Viewer doesn't work, but because the story was never a candidate for it.

What it actually takes to qualify

From working through this, here is the short list I'd check before expecting the Lite Viewer to kick in:

  1. Optimized (Unified) story experience — not Classic.
  2. No Planning or advanced BI features. A Planning model is enough on its own to disqualify the story. For a rolling forecast like mine, that means building a report-only variant on a non-Planning (Analytics) model if you want it to qualify.
  3. New Table Experience for tables. A classic table quietly drops the story out of Lite Viewer eligibility.

The theme across all three: eligibility is decided by the content, not by a setting you flip. And because the fallback is silent, telemetry (System Overview) is the only reliable way to know which viewer really served your story.

Takeaway

If your story is for consumers rather than designers, check Lite Viewer eligibility early — ideally before you invest in per-widget render tuning. In my case the honest result is: this story never qualified, so the Lite Viewer couldn't help it. The next step, when I can rebuild on an Analytics model, is to run a report-only variant through it and measure the real difference — I'll post that comparison when I have it.

A fair caveat: this ran on a trial tenant, and the point here is the routing behavior (which viewer served the story), not an absolute render benchmark — my connection that day was slow enough that timing numbers wouldn't mean much anyway.

Thanks to whoever pointed me to the Lite Viewer — this is exactly the kind of follow-up the comment deserved, even when the answer turned out to be "it didn't qualify."

entry.title: Confluent's New AI Engine Meets SAP: What Changes
entry.content:
Confluent's Real-Time Context Engine reached general availability in May 2026. The premise is clean: instead of an AI agent querying your source systems, or waiting on a batch job, it materializes Kafka topics into a low latency serving layer and exposes them to agents over Model Context Protocol. You enable it on a topic, point an agent at an endpoint, and the agent can read your data.

For anyone who has fought to get SAP data out of the system and into something an application can use, this sounds like the last mile finally getting solved.

I spent a few time testing it against a real SAP table to find out what actually changes. The short version: getting the data to the agent is solved. Getting the agent to understand it is not, and one of the failures is worse than not answering at all.

The setup

One topic, carrying VBAK exactly as it comes out of SAP. Not a curated extract, not a renamed view. The sales document header table, with its real structure, streamed into Confluent Cloud with an Avro schema in Schema Registry.

Three sales orders in it, posted across September, plus one junk record that a test data generator dropped in. I left the junk in on purpose.

Then the Real-Time Context Engine enabled on that topic, and an agent connected over MCP

How the data got there, and why it matters to the argument

The capture side deserves a paragraph, because the whole point of this exercise is what happens when data is genuinely current rather than merely recent.

The topic is fed by application layer business events thanks to OneConnect by Onibex. When a sales document is created or changed in SAP ECC or S/4HANA, the application raises an event, and that event is pushed outbound over an HTTP RFC destination of type G to a gateway, which streams it to Kafka with a registered schema. Nothing polls the database. Nothing runs a delta extractor on a schedule. The update is triggered by the transaction, which matters because a schedule does not know when anything happened. It only knows what time it is.

The implementation here is Onibex One Connect, which I work on. I name it because it is the one whose internals I can describe accurately rather than approximate, and because the capture mechanism is load bearing for the rest of this post. The evaluation questions at the end are the part worth taking away, and they apply whatever produces your topics.

The consequence is that the record the agent reads is the record SAP posted, as of the posting. Not last night's close, not a fifteen minute window. That is the property everyone is chasing, and it is the property that turns the rest of this post from a curiosity into a risk.

The topic list, with the Real-Time Context Engine column on the right.

The engine exposes exactly three tools to the agent: listTopics to discover what exists, getMetadata to read a schema, and queryData to run a read only SQL query against one topic.

What the agent sees

Before anything else, it is worth looking at what getMetadata returns for VBAK, because that is the agent's entire understanding of your data.

One hundred nineteen columns. The names are SAP's, with no descriptions attached. Nine fields called TAXK1 through TAXK9. Five called KVGR1 through KVGR5. KNKLI is the credit control account, CTLPC is the risk category, AMTBL is the released amount, and nothing in the schema says so.

Every date field arrives as VARCHAR: ERDAT, AUDAT, ANGDT, BNDDT, GWLDT, BSTDK, MAHDT, AEDAT. That is faithful to SAP, where DATS is a character type. It is also the root of two of the four problems below.

And no key is declared. Every field is nullable, VBELN included. The only field with a type of its own is the Kafka record key, which is opaque bytes.

What works

A lot, and it is worth being fair about this before the criticism.

Asked for the sales orders, the agent discovered the topic, read the schema, queried it, and came back with a clean table. It recognized the junk record on its own, separated it out, and suggested purging it before the topic feeds anything downstream. That is genuinely good behavior and it took about four seconds.

Three orders and one junk record, discovered and separated without being told.

Filters, ranges, compound predicates and ORDER BY all work. Latency is not the story. The serving problem really is solved.

Where it breaks, in four steps

One: what works by accident.

Filtering a date range works:

WHERE "AUDAT" >= '20260901' AND "AUDAT" <= '20260905'

It returned the right orders. But AUDAT is a string, and this worked only because SAP's DATS format is YYYYMMDD, which happens to sort the same as text and as a date. Point the same engine at a field formatted DD.MM.YYYY and the identical query returns wrong rows with no error at all.

Two: what is refused outright.

SELECT SUM("NETWR") FROM "Oneconnectdemo_VBAK"
QE_UNSUPPORTED_AGGREGATION
"GROUP BY and aggregation functions are not supported."

This is documented and deliberate. No aggregates, no GROUP BY, no joins, no subqueries.

Three: what cannot be expressed at all.

WHERE TO_DATE("AUDAT", 'yyyyMMdd') >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30' DAY
FE_SQL_NOT_SUPPORTED
"Unsupported SQL feature: Function 'TO_DATE' is not supported."

There is no date conversion. Which means "show me the orders from the last thirty days" cannot be formulated against a raw SAP table. That is not an exotic request. It is close to the most common question a sales manager asks.

Four: what fails silently, and this is the one to worry about.

Ask for the orders of customer 1000123. That is how the number appears in an email, on a purchase order, in a conversation.

WHERE "KUNNR" = '1000123'
{"status":"success", "data":[]}

Zero rows. Status success. No error.

With SAP's leading zeros:

WHERE "KUNNR" = '0001000123'

 The order is there.

The first three failures announce themselves. This one answers calmly that the customer has no orders, and the person asking has no way to know the answer is false. Leading zero padding on CHAR fields is exactly the kind of knowledge that lives in an SAP consultant's head and in a data product definition, and that a table extract leaves behind. The agent is not guessing badly. It is guessing reasonably.

The failure I did not expect

Here is where it stops being a list of limitations and becomes something else.

The engine refuses aggregation. Beyond that, the MCP server injects an instruction into the model at connection time. The text is worth quoting exactly:

> "If the user asks for an unsupported operation (aggregation, JOINs, mutations), explain the limitation clearly instead of attempting it. Do not work around unsupported operations by fetching raw data and computing results manually."

So the guardrail exists, and the instruction not to route around it exists.

I asked the agent for the total value of all the sales orders.

It queried the topic. It pulled the rows. It added them up itself. Then, finding one order in USD and two in MXN, it searched the web, took a USD to MXN rate from a financial data site, converted, and returned a single figure: 2,789,118.25 MXN.

The arithmetic is correct. The number is meaningless.

It is meaningless because SAP would not value that order at a market rate pulled from a website. It would use the exchange rate type stored in KURST on the document, against the rate table, on the document's date. The figure the agent produced does not exist in any SAP report, and it never will.

To the agent's credit, it said so, in a line at the bottom that most people will skip: SAP would value that order at the rate type in KURST, so the books may show a different figure.

That caveat is the difference between a careful agent and a reckless one. It is not the difference between a right answer and a wrong one. The number at the top of the response still looks like a fact.

What this actually tells us

The Real-Time Context Engine does what it says. Data reaches the agent in milliseconds, with role based access control and audit logging, without the agent touching the source system. As a serving layer it is solid, and the architecture behind it is sound.

What it does not do, and does not claim to do, is make the data mean anything.

Every one of the four failures above is a semantic failure, not a performance failure. A date stored as text is not a date. A customer number is not a customer number until you know the padding convention. An amount is not comparable to another amount until someone decides which exchange rate applies. None of that is in the schema, so none of it reaches the agent, so the agent fills the gap with the most reasonable assumption available. Sometimes that assumption is right. Sometimes it returns empty. Sometimes it goes to the internet and invents a number.

The uncomfortable part is that real time makes it worse, and this is the argument I did not expect to be making.

A nightly extract is obviously stale, and people treat it accordingly. Nobody commits a credit decision to a number they know is twelve hours old without checking. That skepticism is a safety mechanism, and it is accidental: it exists because the data was slow, not because anybody designed it.

Take the delay away and the skepticism goes with it. An answer that arrives in four seconds, formatted as a table, drawn from an event the ERP raised a moment ago, carries an authority that its semantics have not earned. The pipeline is right about when. It is silent about what. And the freshness is what makes people stop asking.

So the work that real time capture saves you at the transport layer, it hands straight back at the semantic layer, with interest. Getting the event out of SAP the instant it happens is the part that is solved. Making sure the thing that arrives means what a business user thinks it means is the part that is not, and shipping the first without the second is how you build a system that is confidently wrong at speed.

Where this leaves the work

The fix is not a faster engine. It is upstream, in whatever produces the topic.

Publish AUDAT as a date type rather than a character string, and the thirty day question becomes expressible. Normalize the padding on KUNNR when the record is produced, and the customer lookup stops silently failing. Resolve the currency conversion once, in the pipeline, using the rate type on the document, and publish the converted amount as a field. Then the agent is not converting anything, because the answer is already a column.

That is what a declared contract does. It moves the knowledge out of the consumer's assumptions and into the definition, where a functional consultant can review it and disagree with it before an agent ever sees it.

And it costs nothing in freshness, which is the part worth being explicit about. Typing a date, normalizing a padded field and resolving a currency are declarations, not batch steps. They are decided once, when the data product is defined, and applied to each event as it passes. The stream does not slow down because somebody wrote down what AUDAT is. What streams is that declaration made live, which is a very different thing from a pipeline that happens to be fast.

For anyone evaluating this: the question to ask is not how fast the context arrives. It is what your agent will assume about every field where your schema is silent, and whether you would be comfortable with that assumption appearing in a number somebody acts on.

What this test does not cover

This ran against one table, in a demo environment, with four records. I did not measure throughput or latency under load, and no figure here should be read as a benchmark.

I tested a single agent. A different model, or one given a system prompt that enforces the tool's constraints more firmly, might refuse the aggregation instead of computing it. The server side instruction is the same for everyone; how strictly a model honors it is not something I can generalize from one run.

The engine is currently AWS only, requires a registered schema on the topic, and its upsert mode requires the record key in raw byte format rather than a registry format. That last constraint is worth checking against how your topics are produced before you plan around it.

Josue Ramirez is a Data and AI Engineer at Onibex, working on SAP streaming integration and semantic layers for ERP data.

entry.title: V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 2) : From Meter Reading Results to Billable Quantities
entry.content:
In this part of the Vehicle-2-Grid blog series, we will look at the rate configurations required to register Meter Reading (MR) results using the relevant Units of Measurement (UoM) and subsequently bill and invoice the Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) installation.

As described in the previous part (Part 1: Business context and device/register configuration), for each set-up there will be two registers measuring in Kilowatt-hours (kWh) and one in minutes (MIN). We also established that the two kWh registers have a bidirectional relationship: one represents the energy consumed during charging, while the other represents the energy exported back to the grid during discharging. The register measuring in minutes represents the time during which the vehicle remains connected to the grid and available for the availability bonus.

Given this set-up, three different rates were created to register and transfer the MR results:

1. CO_V2G_E - V2G rate for consumption registration

Register operand: E_V2G_CONS

2. COMP_V2G_E - V2G rate for compensation registration

Register operand: E_V2G_COM

3. TIME_V2G_E - V2G rate for duration - Availability bonus

Register operand: E_V2G_TIME

The first two rates follow the standard principles of IS-U Billing. The QUANTI05 variant will write the info lines for the registered quantities, while QUANTI14 variant transfers the quantities measured in kWh to a separate operand that can later be used to calculate the corresponding amounts.

For this blog, we will focus on the third rate, TIME_V2G_E, to demonstrate how the quantity registered in MIN can be converted to hours (HRS) using standard IS-U configuration.

In essence, the same basic principles apply in the sense that the rate concerned will also use the QUANTI05 in the first rate step. However, the register operand E_V2G_TIME will have “MIN” as its UoM in the operand configuration as illustrated below:

Configuration of operand E_V2G_TIME

As can be deduced from the fourth rate step the measured quantity stored in the register operand E_V2G_TIME is transferred to the normal usage quantity operand E_V2G_TREG using the QUANTI14 variant. This obviously requires to also configure the UoM in “min” for the E_V2G_TREG operand as shown in the image below:

Configuration of operand E_V2G_TREG

Now that the quantity measured in minutes has been registered and transferred by the rate concerned, the next step would be to convert the stored quantity to HRS, since a price/hour will later be applied by a different rate. This can be achieved by adding the QUANTI09 variant to the rate, which allows for a quantity to either be multiplied or divided by any given factor:

In the example for this blog, an operand with type FACTOR called “E_V2G_F60” was configured and was later given a value of “60” in the rate facts:

Configuration of operand E_V2G_F60

Configuration of rate facts in E_V2G_TIME

This rate facts configuration allows the QUANTI09 variant to divide the quantity stored in the E_V2G_TREG operand by a factor of “60”. It is however essential to make sure that the controls for the QUANTI09 variant are set to “division of quantity by factor” in the concerned rate step:

 

The result of this division will be stored in quantity operand “E_V2G_CHR”. Since the QUANTI09 variant does not require for the Input QUANT operand and the output QUANT operand to have a matching UoM, the UoM for this operand can be set to HRS as illustrated below:

Configuration of operand E_V2G_CHR

In summary, the E_V2G_TIME rate is configured such that it allows the system to register and transfer the quantity measured in MIN and ultimately convert it to HRS using the QUANTI09 operand. In that way, we already have determined the number of hours which will later be used to calculate the amount of the availability bonus by another rate also included in the billing schema.

IS-U rate TIME_V2G_E – rate step configuration

With the three rates configured, the next step is to make them available for the respective installations through rate determination before the meter reading results can be entered.

For these rates concerned, three specific rate types were created so that a separate rate determination could be created for each rate:

Rate type configuration in table TE069

Rate determination for charging

Rate determination for discharging

Rate determination for availability bonus

The billing-relevant installation of the V2G-devices can now be realized in the IS-U installations for both scenarios described in the previous chapter:

Scenario 1 – One device with three registers (kWh and MIN)

Scenario 2 – Two devices; one exclusively measuring in kWh, the second one exclusively measuring in MIN

Finally, the MR-results can be entered for both installations.

Installation 4100000512 - two consumptions registered in kWh and one in MIN on the same device:

Installation 4100000513 – two consumptions registered in kWh on device ISU-WALLBOX, one in MIN separately registered on device 1:

When running a billing simulation for both installations, we can conclude that both the quantities registered in KWH and MIN will be correctly written on the billing document:

Billing document 300000006100 – Billing simulation for installation 4100000512

Billing document 300000006101 – Billing simulation for installation 4100000513

As a teaser for the next part of this series, the billing simulations also reveal that our quantities in MIN have been successfully converted to HRS:

Billing document 300000006100

Billing document 300000006101

 

As illustrated by the examples above, both setups allow meter reading results to be entered in both kWh and MIN, reflecting the two business scenarios described above. Now that the metering aspect of our scenarios has been covered, in the next part of this blog series we will focus on configuring a facts permissible rate to bill and invoice these quantities. This includes the quantities registered in kWh as well as the connection time registered in minutes and subsequently converted to hours.

entry.title: Navigating Your Path to SAP Cloud ERP Private: Understanding Three Key Offerings
entry.content:
If you're running SAP ERP on Private Cloud Edition (PCE) today, you've likely heard about a few offerings that can help you plan your transformation journey — or bridge the gap until you're ready. But with SAP Safekeeper, the SAP ERP, private edition, Transition Option, and SAP Cloud ERP Private, Nonproduction Usage all in the conversation, it can be hard to tell which one applies to you.

In this post, I'll break down each offering — what it is, who it's for, and how it fits into your long-term ERP strategy.

The Common Thread

All three offerings support customers on their journey toward SAP Cloud ERP Private. They differ in where customers are today — whether on S/4HANA or SAP ERP (ECC) — and what problem they're solving: business continuity, additional time for transformation, or migration readiness.

Let's look at each one.

1. SAP Safekeeper

Who it's for: SAP Cloud ERP Private customers whose S/4HANA release has entered Customer-Specific Maintenance (CSM) and who meet the applicable Safekeeper eligibility criteria.

SAP S/4HANA releases have a defined mainstream maintenance window. When a customer is running an eligible older release that has moved into CSM, Safekeeper provides a structured cloud service to maintain that environment while the customer upgrades to a current, mainstream-supported release.

Key characteristics:

  • Includes a non-production system

  • Supports eligible SAP S/4HANA releases entering Customer-Specific Maintenance, subject to the applicable Safekeeper eligibility criteria

  • The standard Safekeeper term is up to 27 months

  • SAP S/4HANA 1503 and 1605 can have coverage of up to 48 months

  • Migration support through Cloud Application Services (CAS) or Enhanced Operations Service (EOS), as applicable

  • End state: SAP Cloud ERP Private on a mainstream-supported release

Safekeeper is not a path to stay on old software indefinitely — it's a time-bound bridge to help customers move to a current release.

2. SAP ERP, Private Edition — Transition Option

Who it's for: SAP ERP, private edition customers with complex landscapes who need additional time to complete their transformation to SAP Cloud ERP or SAP Cloud ERP Private.

The Transition Option provides a time-bound subscription for eligible customers whose transformation cannot be completed within the standard timeline. The offering was initially announced for business continuity from 2031 through 2033 and has subsequently been extended through 2035.

Importantly, this is not an extension of on-premise SAP ECC maintenance. Customers must first move the relevant SAP ERP systems to SAP ERP, private edition on SAP HANA by December 31, 2030 to be eligible for the Transition Option.

Key characteristics:

  • Covers eligible SAP ERP / SAP ECC scope under the Transition Option

  • Requires the relevant systems to be moved to SAP ERP, private edition on SAP HANA before December 31, 2030

  • Minimum system size: 2 TB

  • SAP HANA is the supported database

  • The Transition Option is a subscription-based offering, rather than an extension of on-premise SAP ERP maintenance

  • Requires the Max Success Plan, including transformation services

  • Originally planned for 2031–2033; now extended through 2035

  • End state: SAP Cloud ERP or SAP Cloud ERP Private

This is a deliberate, structured extension — not a long-term alternative to modernization. Customers using the Transition Option are expected to continue their transformation to SAP Cloud ERP.

3. SAP Cloud ERP Private — Nonproduction Usage

Who it's for: SAP ERP, private edition customers who want to start their S/4HANA transformation journey while continuing to run their existing SAP ERP environment.

Also sometimes referred to as a "migration SKU," this offering provides customers with nonproduction usage rights for SAP Cloud ERP Private during the transition period.

The idea is simple: customers can establish and use nonproduction SAP S/4HANA environments for activities such as scoping, development, testing, validation, process redesign, and migration preparation, while their existing SAP ERP system continues to support production operations.

Key characteristics:

  • Provides nonproduction SAP Cloud ERP Private usage rights

  • Does not provide production usage rights

  • Can cover an unlimited number of nonproduction systems

  • Nonproduction systems must either be subscribed/provisioned or repurposed from existing infrastructure

  • There is no requirement to wait for the production migration before starting nonproduction activities

  • The transition period can be planned according to the customer's migration needs, subject to the applicable product support/end-of-support timelines

  • Customer manages and executes the migration

  • End state: SAP Cloud ERP Private

This is an accelerator — it lowers the barrier to getting started and allows customers to build migration readiness without having to immediately run full parallel production subscriptions.

Choosing the Right Offering

Here's a simple way to think about it:

If you are… Consider…

On SAP Cloud ERP Private / S/4HANA but on an eligible older release entering CSMSAP Safekeeper
On SAP ERP, private edition and need additional time beyond 2030 to complete your transformationTransition Option
On SAP ERP, private edition and ready to start migration planning and nonproduction S/4HANA activities nowNonproduction Usage (Migration SKU)

Final Thoughts

These three offerings reflect SAP's approach to meeting customers where they are while maintaining a clear direction toward SAP Cloud ERP.

Whether you need release maintenance continuity, additional runway for a complex transformation, or a low-risk way to start migration activities, each offering addresses a different stage of the journey.

The important distinction is that these are not interchangeable offerings:

  • Safekeeper helps customers bridge the gap when their S/4HANA release has entered CSM.

  • Transition Option provides eligible SAP ERP customers with additional time to complete their transformation, now extending through 2035.

  • Nonproduction Usage enables SAP ERP customers to begin their SAP Cloud ERP Private migration activities in nonproduction while continuing to operate their existing ERP environment.

If you have questions about which option applies to your situation, reach out to your SAP account team or transformation advisor.

entry.title: V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 3) : From Measured Quantities to Billing and Invoicing
entry.content:
In the previous chapters, we went through the setup of the V2G-device configurations and the installation of those devices, ultimately allowing us to enter MR results in both kWh for charging and discharging and MIN for the availability bonus.

This chapter will be dedicated to the billing and invoicing aspect of the V2G-installations. As established in the previous chapter, three register-permissible rates were created with the sole purpose of registering the consumptions:

  • CO_V2G_E – Registering and transferring of charging quantity in kWh
  • COMP_V2G_E – Registering and transferring of discharging quantity in kWh
  • TIME_V2G_E – Registering of connection time in MIN and conversion to HRS

Billing schema E_V2G_SCH

Once the register-permissible rates have registered and transferred the quantities, a facts-permissible rate is required to calculate the amounts based on the measured quantities.

In the context of this V2G set-up, a new rate “E_V2G_BILL” was created. All rate steps calculating an amount simply use the QUANTI01 variant which allows for a quantity to be multiplied by a quantity-based price to calculate an amount.

IS-U rate E_V2G_BILL – rate steps

The following IS-U prices were configured in our SAP S/4HANA system and stored in the operands with type QPRICE at rate facts level:

  • E_V2G_C+ – Price for charging at 0,3297 EUR/kWh

  • E_V2G_C- – Price for discharging at -0,40 EUR/kWh

  • E_V2G_TCON – Price for availability bonus at -0,24/HR

Unlike the quantity-based prices used to calculate an amount based on the consumptions registered in kWh, price “E_V2G_TCON” must be configured with a UoM in HRS:

IS-U quantity-based price E_V2GTCON with UoM “hrs”

As established in the previous chapter (V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 2): From Meter Reading Results to Billable Quantities), the quantities originally registered in MIN will already have been converted by rate “TIME_V2G_E”. This allows us to directly apply a price per hour for the availability bonus.

Finally, to store the quantity-based price with a UoM of HRS, the QPRICE operand in which the price will be stored must have a matching UoM:

QPRICE Operand E_V2G_TPR

Overview of the rate facts in E_V2G_BILL:

IS-U Rate E_V2G_BILL – Rate facts within fact group V2G

After configuring the facts-permissible rate that calculates the amounts, a facts-permissible rate type will be required to create the rate determination. For these examples, rate type “E_V2G_EBIL” was created and stored in a RATETYPE operand in the installation facts of both installations for each respective scenario.

Rate determination for IS-U rate E_V2G_BILL

Installation 4100000512:

Installation 4100000512 – Operand E_V2G_RTYP maintained in Installation facts

Installation 4100000513:

Installation 4100000513 – Operand E_V2G_RTYP maintained in Installation facts

The IS-U billing and invoicing runs can now be executed for both installations, regardless of the respective device configuration. When analysing the billing documents, we can now filter for the posting-relevant lines. These lines show the amounts calculated by multiplying the quantities registered in kWh by the corresponding quantity-based prices and, more importantly, the amount calculated based on the number of hours the vehicle has been connected to the grid for the availability bonus.

Scenario 1 – Billing document 100000005504

Scenario 2 – Billing document 100000005503

While we are still looking at the billing process, I would also like to highlight another interesting aspect of the availability bonus, namely the fact that the reimbursed connection time could be limited. As a possible commercial rule, the reimbursed connection time could be limited to 250 hours per month. With the hourly price used in this example, the availability bonus would therefore be capped at EUR 60 per month. This is also something I integrated in the E_V2G_BILL rate by adding the IF01 variant which allows us to compare the values of two quantity operands:

In this example, we compare the hourly quantity stored in operand E_V2G_CHR to the quantity stored in operand E_V2G_T250. The latter is fixed at 250 hours in the rate category facts:

Rate category facts of E_V2G_RC : fixed quantity of 250 hours

If the number of hours registered for the availability bonus exceeds the limit of 250 hours, the amount is calculated based on the fixed quantity of 250 hours stored in E_V2G_T250 (rate step 5). Otherwise, the amount is calculated based on the originally measured number of hours stored in E_V2G_CHR (rate step 7). To illustrate this, if the meter reading result were 18.000 MIN, it would be converted to 300 HRS. In that case, the availability bonus would therefore be calculated based on 250 hours, while the remaining 50 hours would not be included in the calculation.

The example below illustrates what this could look like on a billing document:

Billing document 100000005502 – measured quantity of 18.000 MIN exceeding the 250-hour limit.

Before we move on to the results of the invoicing run for both scenarios, I would like to point out that for these examples I do not intend to apply any taxes for the availability bonus. On top of that, I also wanted to ensure that the lines for the availability bonus would be displayed on a separate line on the print document.

For that reason, I created dedicated FI-CA sub-transactions for the availability bonus:

Table TE305 – Sub-transactions for availability bonus: 0250 (Debit) – 0251 (Credit)

Using dedicated sub-transactions allows the availability bonus to be distinguished from the energy-related charges within the FI-CA and invoicing processes. And of course, these sub-transactions are configured on the lines that calculate the amount for the availability bonus in the E_V2G_BILL rate:

IS-U rate E_V2G_BILL - sub-transactions for availability bonus configured in the rate steps

In addition, a separate tax determination, “V0”, linked to tax code “V0” with a 0% tax rate was configured for the availability bonus. This was done to ensure that the availability bonus remains distinguishable from the discharging remuneration during invoicing and is displayed as a separate line on the print document:

Chart of Accounts 2500 – Account assignment for availability bonus

Tax code V0 – 0% tax rate

For the purpose of this blog, the availability bonus is modelled as a separate remuneration for the availability service rather than as a discount that is simply deducted from the energy charge. The actual tax and accounting treatment would depend on the applicable commercial and regulatory framework and is outside the scope of this blog.

Now we can finally execute the invoicing run and review the results:

Scenario 1 – Print document 2000000226

Scenario 2 – Print document 2000000227

As illustrated by the examples above, the availability bonus is displayed as a separate line on the print document, without any tax amount being calculated.

 

With the billing rate, quantity-based prices and corresponding rate determination configured, the two V2G scenarios can now be billed using the quantities registered by the devices.

The examples demonstrate that standard SAP IS-U billing functionality can be used to calculate amounts for both energy quantities measured in kWh and connection time originally recorded in minutes and converted to hours. The same billing logic can be applied to both device setups, regardless of whether the kWh and MIN quantities are registered by a single device or by separate devices.

Most importantly, both the billing documents and print documents confirm the flow from the original meter reading results through quantity processing and unit conversion to the final calculated amounts. This demonstrates how standard IS-U configuration can be used to model and bill selected commercial aspects of a Vehicle-to-Grid scenario without requiring custom billing and invoicing logic.

In the next chapter, we will explore an alternative solution. Rather than managing the entire V2G meter-to-cash flow in IS-U, we will investigate how Convergent Invoicing can be used to calculate the availability bonus and integrate it with IS-U without having to maintain the MR results recorded in MIN.

entry.title: Preserving PowerDesigner Extended Attributes in erwin: Automating UDP Migration and Validation
entry.content:
Introduction

Data-model migration is often described in terms of entities, attributes, relationships, keys, and data types. However, enterprise data models usually contain much more than their core structural definitions.

PowerDesigner models can contain Extended Attributes that capture additional business and governance metadata such as:

Data OwnershipPersonal Data IndicatorsGovernance Properties
Data classificationBusiness-specific classificationsSource-system metadata
Design statusCreation DateLast Updated Date

When a model is migrated from SAP PowerDesigner to erwin Data Modeler, preserving this metadata becomes an important part of migration fidelity. A model may look structurally correct after migration while still losing a significant amount of business metadata. This article describes an automation approach for converting PowerDesigner Extended Attributes into erwin User-Defined Properties (UDPs), applying the values to the target model, and generating an evidence-based reconciliation report.

The Problem Statement: Structural Migration Is Not Enough

Consider a simplified PowerDesigner entity:

Customer
│
├── Customer_ID
├── Customer_Name
└── Customer_Status

From a structural perspective, migrating this entity and its attributes may appear sufficient. But the PowerDesigner model may also contain Extended Attributes such as:

Data Owner             = Customer Domain
Data Classification    = Internal
Personal Data           = No
Design Status           = Approved
Critical Data           = Yes

These properties are not necessarily represented as normal attributes or columns. They are metadata about the model objects. Therefore, a migration process that validates only: Entity, Attribute, Relationship, Data Type or Key can report a successful migration while these additional properties have been lost.

The objective of the UDP migration layer is therefore to Preserve relevant PowerDesigner Extended Attribute metadata as structured erwin UDPs and verify that the values were actually accepted by erwin.

PowerDesigner Extended Attributes vs erwin UDPs

The two modeling platforms represent custom metadata differently. At a high level:

SAP PowerDesignererwin Data Modeler
Extended AttributeUser-Defined Property (UDP)
Property name/pathUDP name
Property valueUDP value
Object identifierObject-level traceability
Extended Attribute profileUDP definition/value configuration

The migration therefore requires more than copying text from one file to another. A translation layer is required. If I try to showcase the snapshots of the transition between the two tools :

Figure 1 : Snapshot of how SAP PowerDesigner stores the Extended Attributes

Figure 2 : Snapshot of how Erwin Data Modeller stores User Defined Properties

Overall Automation Architecture

The UDP migration component was designed as a separate processing layer within the broader PowerDesigner-to-erwin migration framework. The relevant flow can be summarized as:

PowerDesigner
Extended Attribute
        │
        ▼
Extraction
        │
        ▼
Property Mapping
        │
        ▼
UDP Definition
        │
        ▼
UDP Value
        │
        ▼
erwin Data Modeler

The important design principle is that the process does not simply assume that a write operation succeeded. Instead: Write → Read Back → Compare → Report. This makes the migration auditable.

Step 1 — Extracting Extended Attributes from PowerDesigner

The first step is to parse the PowerDesigner model and identify its Extended Attributes.

Figure 3 : Extended Attributes represented in the PowerDesigner LDM XML

The extraction component reads the PowerDesigner model and builds a baseline containing information such as:

Object ID
Entity Name
Entity Code
Extended Attribute Name
Extended Attribute Value

For Example :

Object:
    Customer

Extended Attributes:
    Data Owner        → Customer Domain
    Design Status     → Approved
    Personal Data     → No

The extraction layer also creates an Extended Attribute profile. This profile records information such as:

  • Property name
  • Observed values
  • Number of distinct values
  • Coverage
  • Source property path

This gives the next stage enough information to prepare the target UDP definitions.

Step 2 — Preparing the UDP Schema

Once the Extended Attributes have been extracted, the next step is to determine what UDP definitions are required in erwin. The automation generates a UDP schema containing information such as:

Source Property:
BIM-core.DesignStatus

Target UDP:
DesignStatus

Type:
List

Observed Value:
Approved

The source property path is retained so that the migration remains traceable.

UDP Name Normalization

Source property paths may contain characters that are not appropriate for an erwin UDP name. For example:

BIM-core.DesignStatus -> can be normalized to -> DesignStatus

Similarly, characters that are not suitable for a UDP identifier are normalized. However, simply taking the last portion of a property path can create collisions. For example:

DomainA.Status 
DomainB.Status

would both produce: Status

To avoid this, the automation detects duplicate names and retains additional path information when necessary. This prevents two different source properties from unintentionally mapping to the same target UDP.

Inferring UDP Types

One of the challenges is determining the appropriate erwin UDP type from the source values. The automation uses observed values to make a conservative classification. For example:

Boolean values

If the observed values are: True or False, the property can be represented as a List containing: <True><False>

Small closed value sets

If a property has a small number of distinct values: <Approved><Draft><Deprecated>. It can be represented as a List.

Free-form values

Properties containing arbitrary text are represented as Text. The implementation intentionally avoids aggressively converting digit-looking strings into numeric values. For example: <2021.2> could represent a version rather than a numeric measurement. Treating it as a number could change the original meaning. Therefore, preserving the original value as text is safer.

Step 3 — Building the Property Manifest

After creating the UDP schema, the process creates a property manifest. The manifest effectively becomes the instruction set for the injection stage.

A simplified example looks like:

PD Object ID       : 1234-5678
Entity Name        : Customer
UDP                : DesignStatus
Source Path        : BIM-core.DesignStatus
Value              : Approved

Another record could be:

PD Object ID       : 1234-5678
Entity Name        : Customer
UDP                : DataOwner
Source Path        : BIM-core.DataOwner
Value              : Customer Domain

This separation is useful because it divides the process into two concerns:

What UDPs should exist?
        ↓
UDP Schema

What values should be applied?
        ↓
Property Manifest

Step 4 — Preparing the erwin Model

The next stage works with the erwin model. The migration utility framework can use erwin automation interfaces where available. Because erwin automation is environment-dependent, the overall migration workflow deliberately keeps the hand-off explicit. The model is prepared first, and the UDP injection stage then operates against the appropriate erwin artifact.

This is particularly important in enterprise environments where:

  • erwin may only be available on Windows
  • COM automation may be required
  • licensing may be environment-specific
  • interactive/manual hand-offs may still exist

The automation therefore does not fabricate a target model when erwin is unavailable. Instead, the workflow records the required manual action and continues when the required artifact becomes available.

Step 5 — Creating UDP Definitions in erwin

The loader performs two related tasks.

First: Create or update the UDP definitions

The process checks whether the required UDP exists for the relevant erwin owner type. For example: Entity, Model, Business Glossary etc. The UDP dictionary is then updated as required.

Second: Apply the values

Once the UDP definitions are available, the property manifest can be applied to the corresponding objects. Conceptually:

UDP Schema
     │
     ├── Create UDP
     ├── Configure Type
     └── Configure Values

Property Manifest
     │
     ├── Locate Object
     ├── Set UDP Value
     └── Read Back Value

Step 6 — Writing and Reading Back Values

A major design decision in this implementation is that a successful API call is not considered sufficient proof of migration. For every migrated property, the process records what happened.

The flow is:

Source Value
     │
     ▼
Write to erwin
     │
     ▼
Read value back
     │
     ▼
Compare
     │
     ▼
Record result

This produces statuses such as:

Applied - Verified
Applied - Value Altered
Applied - Not Verified
Skipped - Entity Not Found
Skipped - Property Rejected

This distinction is valuable during large migrations. For example:

Applied - Verified : means that the target value was successfully read back and matched the source.

Applied - Not Verified : means that the process cannot prove that the target contains the expected value. These should not be treated as equivalent.

Source-to-Target Reconciliation

The reconciliation stage joins the source manifest with the actual injection results. A simplified reconciliation table looks like this:

Entity UDPSource ValueTarget ValueStatus
CustomerDesignStatusApprovedApprovedApplied - Verified
CustomerDataOwnerCustomer DomainCustomer DomainApplied - Verified
ProductDesignStatusDraftDraftApplied - Verified
AccountDataClassificationInternalInternalApplied - Verified

This provides an object-level audit trail. The result is not merely: Migration Successful. Instead it answers :

Which property?
On which object?
What was the source value?
What did erwin contain?
Did the values match?
If not, why?

Key Benefits

  • Parses PowerDesigner Extended Attributes directly from the model XML, including source paths for traceability
  • Converts Extended Attributes into appropriately represented erwin UDPs
  • Detects potential naming collisions during UDP normalization
  • Uses conservative type inference rather than blindly converting values
  • Distinguishes real object definitions from object references during parsing
  • Maintains source-to-target object traceability
  • Writes UDP values to erwin and reads them back for verification
  • Produces an object-level source-to-target reconciliation rather than only a pass/fail result
  • Separates genuine exceptions from expected differences such as intentionally empty values
  • Generates structured Excel evidence covering definitions, values, and exceptions
  • Keeps human review in the loop for authoritative metadata definitions and environment-dependent operations
  • Provides a standalone metadata-migration and validation layer that can operate independently of the broader structural migration process

Conclusion

PowerDesigner-to-erwin migration involves more than transferring the structural definition of a data model. Extended Attributes can contain important business, governance, ownership, classification, and lifecycle information. If this metadata is not considered explicitly, a structurally correct migration can still result in information loss. By mapping PowerDesigner Extended Attributes to erwin UDPs, the migration process can preserve this additional metadata in a structured form.

PowerDesigner Extended Attributes
              ↓
          Extraction
              ↓
        UDP Preparation
              ↓
       Property Manifest
              ↓
       erwin UDP Injection
              ↓
          Read Back
              ↓
      Source/Target Compare
              ↓
       Excel Evidence Report

The key is not merely automation. It is automation with verification and evidence that is not simply to move properties from one tool to another, but to preserve their meaning, traceability, and verifiable state in the target model. That makes the approach suitable for repeatable enterprise data-model migration, where traceability, auditability, and metadata fidelity are as important as structural correctness. Thank You…

entry.title: Agentic AI Needs an Environment: Lessons from PaPM and ERP Controlling
entry.content:
For an AI to be truly agentic, it needs an environment to work in. To me, this is almost self-evident.

Connecting an LLM to data is not enough. The environment needs state, business logic, functions the agent can call, and a way to receive feedback from a human. Only then can the AI do more than answer a question. It can move toward a goal: look at what is happening, decide what to do next, run the right function, inspect the result, spot a problem, form a hypothesis, and test it.

By this definition, both a calculation model in SAP Profitability and Performance Management (PaPM) and the Controlling module in ERP can serve as environments for agentic AI.

1. The PaPM calculation model as an environment

In PaPM, the calculation is stored in a narrative form. Functions embed the methodology, and the methodology consists of a preparation phase and the factor analysis calculation itself.

So where does the agentic part come in? I don’t see our agent as a chat that looks at a final table and writes a nicely worded report. Imagine it receives a task: run the calculation and analyze the significant variances for a specific production order. The agent then works out the steps on its own. It prepares the required data, runs the right functions, executes the calculation, looks at the result, and only then starts analyzing. Along the way it can:

  • determine which preparation functions need to run,
  • execute the right sequence of functions,
  • retrieve the result,
  • walk through the final table and find significant variances,
  • identify which factor drove each variance,
  • trace back through the model and methodology to understand how the number was produced,
  • prepare a final report for the user.

Suppose the agent notices that the standard price differs sharply from the actual one. It digs into the drivers and finds that one factor is the number of hours: 170 working hours were expected, but only 10 hours were allocated to this production order.

Context matters here. We are looking at a single production order, but cost allocation happens during period-end closing. If more production orders had been closed in the period, the costs (specifically labor costs) would have been spread across them, and the result for this order would look different.

So the agent doesn’t just say, “You have 170 planned hours against 10 actual.” It explains why this affected the result and how the figure connects to the calculation methodology: the gap between expected and allocated hours changed the cost distribution and, in turn, the outcome of the factor analysis.

When the model isn’t enough

Sometimes the information inside the PaPM model is not sufficient to find the real cause. This is where I also see agentic behavior. The agent must not invent a cause and present it as fact. It should say something like:

“A possible reason is how the actual production time was recorded in ERP.” (a hypothesis)

Then it needs to figure out how to verify that hypothesis, and tell the human where to look:

“Check production order X in ERP. Review the confirmed production time and the source it came from in the calculation.”

The agent is no longer just answering a question. It is directing a person to what needs to be checked. The person goes to ERP, confirms or rejects the hypothesis, and the loop continues.

This points to an important architectural principle. ERP is our source of truth, so the LLM must never decide on its own that a hypothesis is a fact. Once a human confirms the cause, we can use that information going forward. And we don’t necessarily need to copy ERP data into PaPM or replicate anything. We can create a new view on the PaPM side that gives the agent access to the relevant ERP information. Next time, the agent can consult that source and include it in its analysis.

The full cycle looks like this:

calculation result → model analysis → missing information → hypothesis → next step → verification in ERP → human confirmation → new access to the needed information → next analysis with that context

That, for me, is where agentic AI appears. Not in the LLM’s ability to write fluent text, but in the agent’s ability to understand what to do next, what information it lacks, where to go, what to check, and how to continue once it has an answer. The agent can also do more than analyze a finished result. It can run the calculation itself by executing the sequence of methodology functions in PaPM.

2. The Controlling module in ERP

In ERP this is, in my view, even more obvious. The agent operates inside the system that is the source of truth. It knows which controlling tables exist, what they mean, how they relate, which processes exist, and which functions it can call. So it can perform concrete tasks, not just analyze:

  • create a cost center,
  • check an existing cost center,
  • validate an allocation function,
  • verify that data is configured correctly,
  • execute period-end closing steps,
  • work with reporting and the Review Booklet,
  • search for root causes of variances.

Period-end closing shows this best. The goal is simple to state: close the period. But that is not a single function call. It is a sequence of actions: check that all prerequisites are met, including settlement, then check the data, find errors or blockers, run the necessary functions, verify again, and move on.

When something goes wrong, the agent must decide what to do next. For example:

closing → error in allocation → analyze the allocation function → find a missing cost center → depending on what is being allocated, determine which master data is missing → fix it → rerun allocation → check the result → continue closing

This shows what agentic means: goal → planning → action → observe the outcome → decide what’s next → revise the plan if needed.

Our PaPM agent does exactly the same thing. The difference is only in which functions it runs. In ERP, they belong to a business process such as period closing. In PaPM, they belong to the calculation model, accessed through Joule for PaPM and then through Joule Work, a kind of universal workstation connected to the different systems in the landscape.

3. So what is the difference between PaPM and ERP?

For me, the difference is not that one scenario is agentic and the other isn’t. Both can be. The environments are simply different.

In ERP, the agent sits where the business state and the source of truth live, so it doesn’t need extra views to reach the root cause. In PaPM, the agent has the calculation model, methodology, functions, and results, but part of the information needed to explain a root cause lives in ERP. At some point the agent may conclude: “I understand the calculation, but I lack the information to explain the cause.” Then it has to go further.

Put simply:

  • ERP tells us what is happening in the business.
  • PaPM shows how the calculated result was produced.
  • The agent works out why the result looks the way it does, what is missing, and what to do next.

Why this is more than an “analytical assistant”

I wouldn’t call this agent merely an analytical assistant. Yes, it helps users with analytics, but the core idea is different.

Today, a person walks through multiple transactions, exports several Excel files, compares tables, calculates things, finds a variance, goes to another system to verify the cause, and finally assembles a report. The point of an agent is to take the human out of that routine sequence of actions.

The same goal applies to an agent handling period closing. Today a person runs the functions, checks the results, hunts for errors, and decides what to do next. The agent should do that work instead.

That is why I see no fundamental difference between these two flows:

closing → run allocation → check → run settlement → check → finish closing

run PaPM preparation phase → run calculation → review result → find variance → understand cause → request additional information → verify it → continue analysis

Behaviorally, it is the same logic: there is a goal, there is a set of available actions, and the agent chooses what to do next, observes the result, and continues.

This is also why I believe that preparing an important prerequisite for the calculation with a colleague was a real step forward. Yes, a person can walk through transactions and export a number of Excel files to build a report. But then the question is: why do we need an agent at all? The answer is that a person should no longer have to do this. The agent should own the whole process.

The idea may not have been fully understood at first, because it is somewhat indirect. I am not trying to build yet another chat that tells users a nice story about what happened. I want an assistant that performs the sequence of actions a human performs today.

The LLM is there to understand context, interpret information, form hypotheses, decide on next steps, and connect different sources. ERP and PaPM remain the systems that hold the business itself and the calculation logic.

That is why I see agentic AI as an intelligent layer on top of existing systems, not a replacement for them. That, in the end, is the whole point.
