entry.title: Migrating SAP PowerDesigner Metadata to erwin Data Modeler: A Practical XML-Based Approach
entry.content:
Introduction

Data-model migration is not only about moving entities, attributes, relationships, and physical structures from one modelling platform to another. In enterprise data models, metadata such as comments, descriptions, and annotations often contains valuable business and technical context. Losing this information during migration can make the target model structurally complete but less informative and harder to understand.

As part of a PowerDesigner-to-erwin migration scenario, I needed a way to transport selected metadata from a SAP PowerDesigner Logical Data Model (.ldm) into an erwin Data Modeler XML export. The approach described in this article uses Python to read the PowerDesigner XML, match PowerDesigner objects with their corresponding erwin objects, and inject the required metadata into the erwin XML.

The solution currently implements three mappings:

SAP PowerDesigner Comment      → erwin Definition
SAP PowerDesigner Description   → erwin Note: [DESCRIPTION] ...
SAP PowerDesigner Annotation    → erwin Note: [ANNOTATION] ...

The implementation supports both entities and attributes. The major objective behind the python utility was therefore to build a focused metadata migration utility that could:

  1. Read metadata from a PowerDesigner .ldm file.
  2. Identify the corresponding entity or attribute in erwin.
  3. Transform the metadata according to the required mapping.
  4. Preserve existing erwin metadata.
  5. Avoid creating duplicate entries.

The Source System: SAP PowerDesigner

The source of the metadata is a PowerDesigner Data Model (Let, Logical Data Model.ldm).  For each entity and attribute, the script reads:

NameCodeCommentDescriptionAnnotation

Internally, these values are represented using a PDObject structure:

@dataclass
class PDObject:
    name: str
    code: str
    comment: str
    description: str
    annotation: str

The PowerDesigner reader processes entities and their EntityAttribute objects and stores them for subsequent matching.

PowerDesigner Metadata
Figure 1: Comment metadata in SAP PowerDesignerFigure 2: Description metadata in SAP PowerDesigner.Figure 3: Annotation metadata in SAP PowerDesigner.
RTF Metadata Handling

One additional consideration is that PowerDesigner can store metadata fields such as Comment, Description, and Annotation as rich-text/RTF content. The migration utility therefore performs an RTF-to-text conversion before writing the values into erwin. Conceptually, the process is:

PowerDesigner RTF -> strip_rtf() -> Readable plain text -> erwin XML

The script includes a dependency-free strip_rtf() implementation for this conversion. This ensures that formatting/control information from the source is not simply copied as raw RTF into the target metadata.

The Three Metadata Mappings

The core of the solution is the mapping layer. The three mappings are explicitly defined in the script and can also be selected independently through the command line.

Mapping 1: Comment to Definition

The first mapping transfers:

PowerDesigner Comment
        ↓
erwin Definition

The target XML structure is:

<EntityProps>
    <Name>CUSTOMER</Name>
    <Definition>Customer master information</Definition>
    ...
</EntityProps>

The same concept applies to attributes through AttributeProps. The script inserts the <Definition> element immediately after the object's <Name> element. This corresponds to the expected location in the erwin XML structure.

Important behavior

The script does not overwrite an existing Definition. Before inserting the element, it checks whether a Definition already exists. If one is present, the insertion is skipped. This helps prevent accidental replacement of existing target metadata.

Mapping 2: Description to [DEFINITION] Note

The second mapping is:

PowerDesigner Description
        ↓
[DESCRPTION] Note

The [DESCRIPTION] prefix makes the origin and purpose of the note identifiable. The script defines this prefix explicitly: DESCRIPTION_NOTE_PREFIX = "[DESCRIPTION]"

Mapping 3: Annotation to [ANNOTATION] Note

The third mapping is:

PowerDesigner Annotation
        ↓
[ANNOTATION] Note

The corresponding prefix is: ANNOTATION_NOTE_PREFIX = "[ANNOTATION]". This allows Description and Annotation notes to remain distinguishable after migration.

Viewing the Result in erwin

After migration, the corresponding metadata can be viewed in the erwin model.
Figure 4: Migrated Comment displayed as Definition in erwin. The PowerDesigner Comment is represented as an erwin Definition element.Figure 5: Migrated Description in erwin. The PowerDesigner Description is represented as a [DEFINITION] note.Figure 6: Migrated Annotation in erwin. The PowerDesigner Annotation is represented as an [ANNOTATION] note.Figure 7: Migrated metadata available in the erwin Notes section. The Note representation allows the migrated Description and Annotation to coexist with other existing notes.
Implementation Detail: From Object Matching to erwin Notes

The mapping layer determines which erwin structure receives each source value. In this implementation, the standard import often struggles with missing description and comments from SAP PowerDesigner to Erwin. The Python script steps in here to guarantee the population of metadata in the destination fields.

End-to-end processing sequence

1. Read the PowerDesigner .ldm and collect entity/attribute metadata.
2. Parse the erwin XML export and identify corresponding target objects.
3. Match source and target objects using the identifiers supported by the model.
4. Keep Comment → Definition handling separate from Note creation.
5. Convert source rich text/RTF to readable text where required.
6. Create [DESCRIPTION] and [ANNOTATION] note records.
7. Add only the required Note_List entries to Note_List_Array.
8. Write the updated XML and open it in erwin for validation.

The implementation should check the target object before inserting anything. If the relevant Definition or equivalent labelled note already exists, skip or report the duplicate according to the chosen migration policy. This makes the process safer to rerun.

Constructing the erwin Note Record

A Note is not written as an arbitrary child element containing plain text. The XML export represents each entry through a Note_List element whose payload follows erwin's delimiter-based record format. The utility builds the record fields first, escapes the payload for XML, and then places the entry inside Note_List_Array.

Illustrative Python implementation

def build_note_record(text, author, newline_mode,
                      number=1, guid=None,
                      created=None, modified=None):
    """Build one delimiter-separated erwin note record."""
    now = datetime.now().strftime(TS_FMT)
    fields = [""] * NOTE_FIELD_COUNT

    fields[IDX_NUMBER] = str(number)
    fields[IDX_CREATED] = created or now
    fields[IDX_CREATOR] = author
    fields[IDX_MODIFIED] = modified or now
    fields[IDX_MODIFIER] = author
    fields[IDX_TEXT] = encode_note_payload(text, newline_mode)
    fields[IDX_FLAG] = NOTE_FLAG_DEFAULT
    fields[IDX_GUID] = guid or (
        "{%s}" % str(uuid.uuid4()).upper()
    )

    return SEP.join(fields)


def build_note_element(record, index=0):
    return (
        '<Note_List HandleNonPrintableChar="Y" index="%d">%s</Note_List>'
        % (index, xml_escape_text(record))
    )


def build_note_array(records):
    inner = "".join(
        build_note_element(record, i)
        for i, record in enumerate(records)
    )
    return "<%s>%s</%s>" % (
        NOTE_ARRAY_TAG, inner, NOTE_ARRAY_TAG
    )

Understanding the implementation

The three functions handle different responsibilities:

  • build_note_record() assembles the individual fields of an erwin Note record, including the note number, creation and modification timestamps, creator, modifier, note text, flag, and GUID.

  • build_note_element() wraps the generated record in a Note_List XML element, applies the expected attributes, and escapes the content for XML.

  • build_note_array() combines the individual note elements into the enclosing Note_List_Array structure.

The constants and helper functions—such as NOTE_FIELD_COUNT, IDX_TEXT, SEP, NOTE_ARRAY_TAG, encode_note_payload(), and xml_escape_text()—must be defined according to the record layout verified in the target erwin XML export. The field positions, payload encoding, and GUID placement should not be inferred from a generic XML example.

Why Byte-Level XML Splicing?

One of the key implementation decisions is that the script does not simply parse the complete erwin XML and serialize it again. Instead, it uses an XML parser to locate the exact positions where changes are required, and then performs targeted modifications against the original byte stream. The reason is preservation. A normal XML round-trip can change aspects of the original file, such as:

  • Line endings
  • Empty-element representation
  • Namespace declaration formatting
  • Other serialization details

The script therefore uses Expat to identify byte offsets and then performs byte-level splicing. Content outside the modified regions remains byte-for-byte unchanged.

XML-Level View
Figure 8: XML-level representation of the migrated metadata. This provides a useful way to understand the difference between the source PowerDesigner metadata and the final erwin XML representation.

Conclusion

Preserving metadata during model migration is essential for maintaining context and traceability between the source PowerDesigner model and the target erwin model. This approach maps PowerDesigner Comments, Descriptions, and Annotations to corresponding erwin Definitions and Notes, while retaining existing metadata and minimizing changes to the original erwin XML. By using object-level matching and controlled XML updates, the approach provides a practical way to automate metadata migration while keeping the resulting erwin model traceable to its PowerDesigner source.

Key Benefits

  • Preserves PowerDesigner metadata
  • Maps Comments to erwin Definitions
  • Maps Descriptions and Annotations to structured Notes
  • Retains existing erwin Notes
  • Supports entity- and attribute-level matching
  • Provides migration statistics and optional CSV reporting
  • Protects the original erwin XML structure through byte-level updates
  • Can be integrated into broader PowerDesigner-to-erwin migration workflows

The broader lesson to convey is pretty straightforward: "A successful data-model migration should preserve not only the structure of the model, but also the metadata that explains and gives context to that structure." Thank You..

entry.title: V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 4): Calculating the availability bonus in Convergent Invoicing
entry.content:
Introduction

In the previous chapters of this series, we explored how a Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) meter-to-cash process can be implemented entirely within SAP IS-U, including the calculation of an availability bonus based on the time a vehicle remains connected to the grid during discharging.

In this final chapter, I would like to explore an alternative approach: leveraging SAP Convergent Invoicing (CI) to calculate the availability bonus while keeping the conventional IS-U metering and billing setup unchanged. Instead of introducing additional configurations in IS-U to register meter-reading results in minutes (MIN), we can use CI to calculate the availability bonus based on the number of hours for which the vehicle was connected to the grid.

Meanwhile, the charging and discharging quantities continue to be registered through a conventional bidirectional meter in kilowatt-hours (kWh).

In other words, our IS-U installation requires only the conventional bidirectional-meter setup for the Meter-to-Cash process.

Bidirectional meter ISU_WALLBOX01 installed in installation 4100000514.

MR-results for charging and discharging registered in kWh.

Billing document 100000005601 – No amount calculated for availability bonus.

The availability bonus will be calculated separately in CI and subsequently integrated into the IS-U invoicing process. But how can we bring these two billing streams together and ensure that the customer receives a single invoice covering both the energy-related charges and the availability bonus?

Let's explore the required configuration and processing steps, from creating and rating consumption items in CI to joint invoicing and the resulting FI-CA postings.

 

1. Consumption Item Class (CIC) and Billable Item Class (BIC) creation

The first step is to configure a new Consumption Item Class (CIC). As a demonstration for this blog, I created a new CIC named “ZV2G”, specifically for the V2G solution.

Customizing path:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Basic Functions >> Consumption Items >> Consumption Item classes >> Maintain Consumption Item Classes

Consumption Item class ZV2G

Consumption Item class ZV2G – Interface components.

Once the CIC has been created and its interface generated, the system creates a corresponding database table. In this example, the generated table is /1FC/0ZV2G400.

Consumption Item class ZV2G generated database table - /1FC/0ZV2G400.

This table stores the consumption items belonging to the class, including items created for testing and simulation. After rating, the corresponding rating results can be examined in the relevant records.

Examples of entries created after simulation runs.

Once the consumption items (CIT) have been rated, the system generates the resulting billable items, which can be processed further in Convergent Invoicing through billing execution. For this scenario, however, I also configured integrated billing, which allows the billing document to be created as part of the rating process in my setup.

To support the V2G integration, I created a corresponding Billable Item Class (BIC), also named ZV2G.

Customizing path:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Basic Functions >> Billable Items >> Billable Item classes >> Maintain Billable Item Classes

Billable Item class ZV2G.

Billable Item class ZV2G – Database table /1FE/0ZV2G4IT00.

Billable Item class ZV2G – interface components.

It is important to note that this V2G blog post does not aim to explain every aspect of CIC and BIC configuration. The exact configuration depends on the intended integration scenario, the selected interface components, and the requirements of the implementation.

However, for a more detailed introduction to Convergent Invoicing and its integration with Utilities, I highly recommend the blog series by Oleh Korolyk, beginning with his article:

SAP Billing and Revenue Innovation Management: commodity and non-commodity services on one (or separate) invoice is no longer a dream

The article provides an excellent starting point and contains all the links to all other posts in his series.

I highly recommend reading this blog series as well!

2. Pricing and Rating Configurations

As discussed in the previous chapter, the availability bonus in our example is calculated using a price of −0.24 per hour (HR).

To implement this calculation in Convergent invoicing, I configured a pricing procedure for the relevant posting area 8200. This can be done by following the customizing path below:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Basic Functions >> Pricing >> Assigning Pricing schemas

For this example, I used pricing procedure CI1001, which is an SD pricing procedure that can be maintained using transaction V/08. A pricing procedure defines the sequence of condition types and calculation steps used to determine the applicable price.

Pricing procedures CI1001 with the condition types configured in its steps.

For this example, I used condition type PST0 to maintain the price applied when rating the consumption items. The condition record can be maintained using transaction VK11, with the relevant combination of sales organization, distribution channel, customer, material, and price unit, according to the condition type configuration.

Price condition within condition type PST0.

Configurations of material EXTM – Transaction MM03.

Once the SD pricing configuration is complete, we must ensure that the relevant pricing logic is executed when the consumption items are rated.

 For this purpose, I assigned the function module ‘FKK_BIX_RATING_EVENT_30_SD’ in the program extensions of the newly created rating group RV2G.

Customizing path:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Rating >> Define Rating Groups

I then assigned our newly created Consumption Item Class ZV2G to the rating group RV2G:

Customizing path:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Rating >> Assign Consumption Item Classes to Rating Groups

With these settings in place, the consumption items can be rated using the configured pricing logic.

The negative price represents the customer credit in this example. The resulting amount must be verified against the actual pricing and posting configuration to ensure that the availability bonus is represented correctly in the subsequent billing and FI-CA documents.

3. Provider contract for the availability bonus

After completing the required CI configuration, we can create the provider contract for the relevant business partner. For this purpose, I used transaction FP_VT1.

The provider contract must contain the relevant account and commercial assignments required by the pricing and rating configuration. In this example, these include the business partner, contract account, company code, sales organization, distribution channel, and material.

Provider contract V2G_AVLB – General Data.

The provider contract V2G_AVLB is linked to contract account 200000003200.

Provider contract V2G_AVLB – General Data: Linked to contract account 200000003200.

In the account assignment data, the provider contract is linked to sales organization 2510, company code BCMP, and product EXTM.

Provider contract V2G_AVLB – Account Assignment: Linked to Sales org. 2510; Company code BCMP and Product EXTM (MM).

These assignments allow the consumption items to be associated with the relevant customer account and commercial data used for pricing.

4. Creation and Rating of Consumption Items

Once the provider contract has been created, we can create a consumption item using transaction FKKBIXCIT_CWB.

 For this demonstration, I created the consumption item manually and linked it to the provider contract. The following information can then be specified:

  • Consumption date
  • Unit of measurement (UoM)
  • Quantity consumed
  • Consumption item type

The unit of measurement (UoM) specified in the consumption item must be compatible with the pricing configuration. Since our availability bonus is calculated per hour, I used HR as the unit of measurement.

Consumption Item 2608230005000000600001

In this example, we create the consumption items manually. In a production environment, however, consumption items would typically be created automatically from data received from an external application. For example, a charging station provider could supply the connection duration of a vehicle through an integration interface.

The interface would need to transform and validate the incoming data before creating the corresponding consumption items in your SAP S/4HANA system.

SAP provides APIs for creating consumption items. The exact API to use depends on the interface generated for the consumption item class and the SAP release. For the ZV2G class, the generated interface and its supported usage should be verified before implementation.

One option would be the general API ‘FKK_BIX_CIT_CREATE_API ‘:

Function Module FKK_BIX_CIT_CREATE_API in which function ‘FKK_BIX_CIT_CREATE’ is called.

Alternatively, SAP can generate a class-specific RFC function module for each Consumption Item Class, following the naming convention /1FC/XXX_CIT_CREATE_API. These generated interfaces are adapted to the structure of the corresponding class.

For our example, after generating the interfaces for CIC ZV2G, the system created the Function Module ‘/1FC/ZV2G_CIT_CREATE_API’, which is tailored to the structure of CIC ZV2G.

Function Module /1FC/ZV2G_CIT_CREATE_API adapted to the structure of CIC ZV2G.

Once the Consumption Item has been created, we can execute rating.

After successful rating, the consumption item receives the corresponding rated status:

Consumption item 2608230005000000600001 with status “Rated”.

In a conventional CI process, rating produces billable items that are subsequently processed during billing. As mentioned before, in my example, the rating group is configured for integrated billing, so the billing document is created as part of the configured rating process.

Consequently, there is no need to execute a separate billable-item billing run using transaction FKKBIXBIT_MON for this particular scenario.

This behavior depends on the integrated-billing configuration and should not be assumed for every CI implementation:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Rating >> Define Rating Groups

The resulting billing document contains the calculated availability bonus. It also carries the quantity and unit of measurement entered in the consumption item, provided the relevant billing-quantity interface component is selected in the billable item class.

Billing document 347 including amount, quantity, and unit of measurement.

Billable Item Class ZV2G with interface component “Billing quantity”.

This completes the CI calculation of the availability bonus. The next step is to integrate the resulting billing document into the IS-U invoicing process.

5. Executing the invoicing run in IS-U

We now have two billing documents:

  • An IS-U billing document containing the charging and discharging quantities measured in kWh.
  • A CI billing document containing the availability bonus calculated from the connection duration.

The objective is to process both documents through IS-U invoicing so that the resulting customer invoice includes both components.

To ensure that both billing documents can be invoiced together, you need to customize the invoicing process in which you can specify the source document categories in the selection control.

Once your invoicing process is defined in the customizing, you also need to specify to which creation reason in IS-U it applies. For our scenario, we want our CI billing document to be invoiced on the same print document together with an IS-U billing document with source document type “01”:

EAINV_MON – Source document type.

When you invoice the contract account via transaction EAINV_MON, you will be asked to specify the invoicing process along with its compatible creation reason. After executing, the system will at one point call function ISU_INV_SELECT_DOCUMENTS which verifies whether the selected invoicing process is compatible with the creation reason of the IS-U billing document:

Function Module ISU_INV_SELECT_DOCUMENTS with CALL FUNCTION ‘ISU_DB_TE2602_SELECT’ on line 82.

As illustrated by the image above, the assignment between the creation reason and the invoicing process is stored in table TE2602:

Table TE2602: Assignment of invoicing procedure to creation reason.

If the required assignment is missing, the CI billing document may not be selected for joint invoicing through the intended IS-U invoicing process.

The relevant customizing activity is:

SAP Customizing Implementation Guide >> SAP Utilities >> Invoicing >> Integration with Convergent Invoicing >> Invoicing of Source Documents from Convergent Invoicing >> Assign Invoicing Process to Reasons for Creation

Once the required configuration is in place, the joint invoicing run can be executed. In my example, both transactions EAINV_MON and EA19 can be used to produce the joint invoicing result:

Joint invoicing of billing documents 347 (CI) and 100000005601 (IS-U) through EAINV_MON.

Joint invoicing of both billing documents 347 (CI) and 100000005601 (IS-U) through EA19.

Although both transactions produce the same result, I prefer EAINV_MON because it displays additional information such as target process. 

After executing the invoicing run and selecting the relevant source documents, the system successfully creates IS-U print document 2000000229:

Application log – print document 2000000229 successfully created.

By navigating to the Source Documents tab of the print document, we can identify the billing documents included in the invoicing process. In this example, the print document references the IS-U billing document 100000005601 (ERCH) and the CI billing document 347 (INVBI):

IS-U Print Document 2000000229 with source documents 100000005601 (ERCH) and 347 (INVBI).

This confirms that the two billing results have been brought together in a common IS-U invoicing process.

6. Final results: IS-U print document, Invoicing document and FI-CA posting documents

After successful joint invoicing, we can examine the resulting documents to understand how the IS-U and CI components are represented in the system.

6.1 IS-U Print Document

The resulting IS-U print document is 2000000229.

Its document overview shows the posting-relevant items originating from the IS-U billing process and the availability bonus calculated through CI.

IS-U Print document 2000000229 - Document Overview.

As shown in the image above, I did not apply any tax amounts for the availability bonus just as I did in the previous part of this series (V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 3) : From Measured Quantities to Billing and Invoicing). For the invoicing document that will be created through CI, you can configure this in posting area 2610 by linking the required tax determination to your company code, main and sub-transactions and the targeted G/L account for postings to be made.

Account assignments on chart of accounts 2500 in posting area 2610.

6.2. CI Invoicing Document

The IS-U print document also provides a link to the associated CI invoicing document.

In this example, the CI invoicing document number is 7000000116. It can be identified through the relevant reference field in table ERDK in the demonstrated system.

Invoicing document 7000000116 in table field ERDK- INVDOCNO.

To examine the document in more detail, we can use transaction FKKINVDOC_DISP.

The CI invoicing document contains the relevant invoicing information for the availability bonus, including the items processed through CI and the applicable integration information.

Invoicing document 7000000116 in FKKINVDOC_DISP.

This provides a useful way to trace the availability bonus from its original consumption item through rating and billing to the final invoicing result.

6.3. FI-CA Posting Documents

Finally, we can examine the FI-CA postings created as part of the invoicing process.

In this example, the system creates two FI-CA posting documents: one for the items originating from IS-U and another for the availability bonus originating from CI.

The documents are 5000000702 and 5000000703, and both refer to the common IS-U print document 2000000229:

Two documents posted in FI-CA:  5000000702 and 5000000703.

Table DFKKOP: posting documents 5000000702 and 5000000703 representing the total amount of IS-U print document 2000000229.

This distinction is important. Although the customer-facing result is a common IS-U print document, the underlying financial processing can retain separate FI-CA documents for the IS-U and CI components.

The example therefore illustrates how the availability bonus can be calculated independently in CI and integrated into the IS-U invoicing process without requiring both components to originate from the same billing engine.

 

Conclusion

With this final chapter, we have explored an alternative approach to integrating a V2G availability bonus into the SAP IS-U Meter-to-Cash process by leveraging Convergent Invoicing.

By retaining the conventional IS-U metering and billing setup for charging and discharging quantities in kWh, we can calculate the availability bonus separately in CI based on the vehicle's connection time. The resulting CI billing document can then be integrated into the IS-U invoicing process, allowing both billing results to be included in a common IS-U print document.

We have also followed the process beyond billing and invoicing, examining the resulting CI invoicing document and the separate FI-CA postings generated for the IS-U and CI components.

This approach demonstrates one possible way to combine the capabilities of SAP IS-U and Convergent Invoicing while avoiding additional IS-U configuration to register the availability duration in minutes.

I hope this four-part V2G series has provided useful insights into the different possibilities for implementing Vehicle-to-Grid scenarios in SAP Utilities.

Thank you for following the series! I would be very interested to hear your thoughts:

Would you implement the availability bonus directly in IS-U, or would you consider Convergent Invoicing for this purpose?

Feel free to share your experiences and alternative approaches in the comments.

entry.title: Stop Building SAP Apps: Business AI Applications On Demand with an Ontology-Based MCP Server
entry.content:
Apps on demand instead of app projects

A sales rep desk for delivery-blocked orders on SAP ECC took us a few hours to build, not a project. It runs on live SAP data, follows the team's process step by step and writes back to SAP only after the rep confirms.

The usual route looks different. A new cockpit for one team starts a cycle of requirements, functional and technical specifications, OData services, a Fiori or UI5 front end, testing and transports. Weeks pass, and the team keeps working in reports, spreadsheets and email.

We took a typical wholesale scenario, connected Claude Desktop to the Skybuffer AI MCP server, our ABAP add-on, and asked for the application with nothing but the process description. This post shows what came out, the two architectures it runs on, and why the MCP server, more than the AI model, decides whether this works.

The example: a release desk for delivery block 17

The desk works the orders that SAP holds on delivery block 17 ("CSR action: deadline") because their cancel date is close. Each one needs a decision before that date, and the desk takes the customer service rep through all eight steps of the process on one screen, with live SAP data at every step.

The worklist: twelve orders on block 17, sorted by days to the cancel date, with stock coverage per order and a count of orders at each step.

StepWhat the rep sees and doesSkybuffer AI MCP tool
1. IdentifyEvery open order on the block, sorted by days left to the cancel date, with filters for overdue, due within two days and ready to releaseget_blocked_sales_orders
2. Check stockPer line: ordered quantity, available to promise, shortfall and the next incoming receipt; stock on hand per plantget_blocked_sales_orders, get_material_stock
3. DecideSAP's recommendation (release, extend, partial ship or cancel) with a plain-language reason; the rep makes the callget_blocked_sales_orders
4. Contact the customerOne email draft per customer, addressed to the buyer from SAP, covering all of their orders on hold with PO numbers, account executive in copyget_customers_contact_details
5. Customer replyThe answer is logged with a note, and a reply-by date drives a follow-up list(kept by the app)
6. Update SAPNew requested date, rejected lines with a reason, block kept or removed; every change shown in a confirmation dialog first, then read back from SAPchange_sales_order, get_sales_order_status
7. ReleaseBlock 17 removed, the order goes to the warehousechange_sales_order
8. Follow upOrders without an answer by the reply date come back as a chase list(kept by the app)

Steps 2 and 3: availability per line, stock on hand and SAP's recommendation with its reason. Here SAP suggests a partial shipment, and the rep picks the line to cancel.

When stock covers every line before the cancel date, SAP recommends a release instead. The customer doesn't need to hear from us, so the desk skips the email and lets the rep remove the block straight away.

Every line is available before the cancel date, so SAP suggests a release and no customer contact is needed.

Nobody wrote UI code by hand. Claude Desktop generated the application from the eight-step process description and the tool descriptions the MCP server publishes. The first version ran within a few hours of the first prompt, and we refined it over the same day.

Two rules held throughout. Nothing changes in SAP without the rep's confirmation, and customer emails are only drafted, never sent by the app.

Step 4: one draft per customer for all of their orders on hold, with the buyer's address from SAP and the account executive in copy. Nothing is sent from the page.

Step 6: before posting, the rep sees each change in plain words and the exact MCP call behind it.

Why the MCP server needs a business ontology, not an OData wrapper

The model can only build an app as good as the tools it is given. An MCP server that wraps OData services hands the model database entities; an MCP server built on a business ontology hands it the process itself.

By ontology we mean the shared vocabulary of the business: the objects (customer, sales order, line, delivery block, cancel date, availability, inbound receipt), how they relate, the actions allowed on them and the rules behind those actions. When the tools speak that vocabulary, the steps of the app can match the steps of the process one to one.

 OData wrapperBusiness ontology MCP server
A tool representsAn entity set: order headers, items, schedule linesA business capability: find blocked orders and assess them against their cancel date
Who joins the dataThe model, call by call: header, items, schedule lines, availability, stock listThe server, inside SAP, in one call
Business rulesRebuilt by the model each time: confirmations, rejected lines, units of measureImplemented once in ABAP with standard BAPIs
What comes backRaw fields such as VDATU, LIFSK, KWMENGAnswer-ready fields: days to cancel, coverage, next inbound date, recommended action and its reason
WritesA generic update on an entity; the model must know update flags and schedule linesBusiness actions: move the requested date and keep the block, reject lines with a reason, remove the block
AuthorizationsPer servicePer action and per order, checked against the user's SAP roles on every call

The difference shows in the numbers. The desk's worklist of twelve orders, with availability per line and a recommendation per order, comes from a single call. Built on entity reads, the same screen needs several reads per order plus an availability check per line, and every join is a chance for the model to get it wrong.

Every call goes to the live system, so the app works in real time. Nothing is replicated into a data lake or a side database, and SAP stays the system of record.

Architecture 1: the ABAP add-on and Claude Desktop

The simplest setup has two parts: Claude Desktop on the user's machine and the Skybuffer AI MCP server, installed as an ABAP add-on in the SAP system itself.

Architecture 1: Claude Desktop and the ABAP MCP add-on

The rep works in Claude Desktop and signs in to SAP through SSO with their own SAP user, so there is no shared technical user. Every tool call goes over HTTPS to the add-on, which runs the business logic inside SAP with standard BAPIs and checks that user's SAP authorizations before it returns or changes anything.

The add-on's MCP endpoint is an ICF node in the SAP system. Claude reaches it as a remote MCP connector, and connector calls come from Claude's cloud, so the ICF node is published through your reverse proxy or a secure tunnel; in Architecture 2, the gateway takes that role.

There is no middleware to install, no data replication and no separate app server. The add-on runs on SAP ECC and on SAP S/4HANA, with S/4HANA variants where the data model differs, so the app moves with the system through a migration.

This setup suits pilots, departmental apps and any team that wants the shortest path from an idea to a working app.

Architecture 2: SAP BTP with the MCP Gateway in the middle

Companies that standardize on SAP BTP can put the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite, announced at SAP TechEd 2025, between Claude and the add-on. The app and the tools stay exactly the same; the gateway adds central governance.

Architecture 2: SAP BTP with the MCP Gateway in the middle

Claude calls the gateway with the user's identity. The gateway applies its policies and forwards the call through SAP Cloud Connector, and the add-on runs the same tools as in Architecture 1.

What the SAP-endorsed path adds, as SAP's reference architecture describes it:

  • One governed entry point for MCP tools, including external MCP servers such as the Skybuffer AI add-on
  • OAuth 2.0 and OIDC enforcement, rate limiting, payload protection and traffic management
  • Monitoring, distributed tracing and analytics in one place
  • Tool lifecycle from creation to versioning and deprecation, with MCP specification upgrades handled by SAP

The SAP system itself stays behind the firewall: SAP Cloud Connector opens an outbound tunnel to BTP, so no inbound port is needed.

The gateway can also turn existing APIs and integration flows into MCP tools. That is handy for simple reads, but for a process like this one it brings back the OData-wrapper problem. The split that works: the gateway governs the call, and the business ontology lives in the MCP server behind it.

The Skybuffer AI MCP server and its predefined tools

Both architectures run on the same MCP server: the Skybuffer AI MCP server, an ABAP add-on from Skybuffer that implements MCP inside SAP ECC and SAP S/4HANA. It is built on SAP technology only, so any SAP team or partner can support it.

Out of the box, the server comes with predefined business tools. Each one is a business capability, such as reading a customer's contacts, checking stock or creating a purchase requisition, written in ABAP on a common framework and published with a description that tells the model when and how to use it.

Predefined tools are why an app takes hours instead of weeks:

  • Most of the app already exists. The desk reuses predefined tools for customer contacts, stock, order status and governed data access. Only two tools were new for this scenario, get_blocked_sales_orders and change_sales_order, and both are now part of the standard content.
  • Business logic is built once, tested and shared. Availability, confirmations, rejection reasons and units of measure are handled in ABAP with standard BAPIs instead of being reinvented by the model in every app. Two apps never disagree about the same order, and an improvement to a tool reaches every app that uses it.
  • Security comes with every call. Each tool checks the user's SAP authorizations before it reads or changes anything, and changes are recorded in the SAP application log. A new app inherits these controls instead of rebuilding them.
  • IT stays in control. Customizing decides which tools are active and which tables and views the data access tool may read, each with its own field list and record limit.

When a process needs something new, the new tool is one more ABAP class on the same framework, registered in customizing and transported like any other ABAP change. The server publishes it to every MCP client automatically, so the next app can use it the same day.

Distributing the app across the company

The desk is a published page on claude.ai, so rolling it out means sharing a link, not deploying an application. Claude artifacts on Team and Enterprise plans provide everything the rollout needs.

  1. Each user connects the Skybuffer AI connector once in Claude, under Settings > Connectors, and signs in through SSO with their own SAP user.
  2. The author shares the page with named colleagues or with the whole organization. Viewers sign in to Claude, on the desktop app or the web.
  3. An Owner keeps control in the admin settings: artifacts on or off, connector calls from artifacts on or off, and public sharing, which is off by default.

Once shared, these rules hold:

  • Every viewer sees their own SAP. Each connector call runs through the viewer's own connection, so two reps with different SAP roles see different orders. The page never sees credentials, and each viewer approves access before the first call.
  • Actions run as the person who clicks. A release, a new date or a rejected line is posted under that user's SAP account and authorizations.
  • The team shares one picture. Decisions, customer replies, notes and the activity feed are kept with the app, while SAP data is read live for each viewer.
  • Updates reach everyone. Each republish becomes a new version on the same link, and the owner chooses which version viewers see.
  • Governance is built in. Artifacts are visible only to signed-in members of the organization and the people they are shared with, and they fall under retention policies, the audit log and the Compliance API.

Conclusion: fast, cheap and built to SAP standards

With a proper MCP server and Claude Desktop, a business AI app stops being a project. A team describes its process in the morning and works in the app in the afternoon, on live SAP data.

 Classic app projectBusiness AI app on demand
First versionWeeks of specification, development and testingA few hours
Built byA development teamA consultant or power user with Claude Desktop
New to deployOData services, a Fiori or UI5 app, transportsNothing, once the add-on is in place: the app is a shared link
Fit to the processAs specified at the startBuilt from the process description, refined the same day
DataOften copied for reportingLive from SAP ECC or S/4HANA
A changeA change requestA prompt, republished to the same link

Fast. Apps arrive in hours, and changes the same day.

Cheap. Architecture 1 needs no middleware and no extra runtime, only the ABAP add-on in the existing system and Claude for the users. There is no UI code or OData layer to maintain, most tools come predefined with the server, and each new one is reused by the next app.

Very good quality. The logic runs in SAP through standard BAPIs and SAP authorization checks. Every change is confirmed by a person and read back, and the app follows the process because it was built from it.

The same approach works on SAP ECC today and on SAP S/4HANA after the migration. The Skybuffer AI MCP server is not tied to one client either: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and VS Code can all use the same tools. Start with Architecture 1 for speed, and move to Architecture 2 when the rollout needs SAP BTP governance.

entry.title: From Integration to Intelligence :Building enterprise-ready AI agents with Integration Suite & MCP
entry.content:
I have sat through a lot of agent demos this year. The pattern is usually the same. Someone types a request in plain English, the agent reads a purchase requisition, checks a budget, creates a purchase order in S/4HANA, emails the supplier, and posts a cheerful summary. The room claps. It is impressive.

Then I ask the question that integration people always ask: what happens on the 40,000th run? What happens when the supplier endpoint times out, when the mapping changes, when audit wants to know who approved what, or when the token bill arrives at the end of the month?

That is the gap between an agent that works in a demo and an agent that survives production. After close to two decades of building integrations, first on Oracle SOA and OSB, later on Boomi, Apigee and SAP BTP, my view is that the gap is mostly not a model problem. It is an architecture problem. And it is one the SAP integration community is unusually well placed to solve.

Last week I attended SAP's session "Building the Autonomous Enterprise with Integration Suite, AEM, and Agents" (13 October 2026). One line from it has stayed with me, because it captures the whole argument in eight words:

"Let the agent think. Let Integration Suite execute."

This post is my attempt to unpack that line from an architect's point of view: where agents earn their keep, where they should stay out of the way, and how API-centric integration and the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite connect the two.

1. The overloaded agent

When teams first build agents, they tend to give them everything. The agent calls the APIs, builds the payloads, decides on retries, transforms the formats and handles the errors. It feels efficient because there is only one component to think about.

It is not efficient. In effect you are asking a probabilistic reasoning engine to re-implement things your integration platform already does deterministically, with monitoring, retries and audit built in. Mapping JSON to IDoc, routing a message by company code, validating mandatory fields against a schema, sending a payment file over a bank channel: none of these need judgment. They need to be done exactly the same way every time.

The SAP session framed the consequences well, and they match what I have seen in practice:

  • Duplicated capability. The agent rebuilds APIs, EDI handling, mappings and routing you already own.
  • Reduced reliability. Predictable PO, invoice and payment flows start to depend on non-deterministic behavior.
  • Harder governance. Security, auditability and compliance become difficult to standardize when logic lives inside prompts.
  • Blurred accountability. When something fails, is it the reasoning, the integration, the partner or the backend? Nobody can tell quickly.
  • Higher operating cost. Tokens and agent capacity are spent on repetitive plumbing instead of the reasoning you actually wanted.

I like to describe it as driving a Lamborghini to the supermarket. You can, but it is not what the car is for, and the parking is a nightmare.

2. Who should own each step? A Procure-to-Pay test

The most useful part of the session, for me, was a simple step-by-step assessment of a standard Procure-to-Pay flow. For each step, it asked one question: is the value here in reasoning, or in reliable execution? I have adapted it below because I think every team should run this exercise on its own processes before writing a single prompt.

Look at where the "Agent" rows sit. They are at the edges of the process: interpreting demand, explaining approvals, investigating exceptions and analyzing spend. The middle of the process, where money and goods actually move, belongs to integration. The three-way match is the interesting one. The match itself is a rule. The moment it fails, though, someone has to work out why, and that is exactly the kind of work an agent is good at.

So the question is not "agent or integration?" It is "which part of this step needs judgment?"

3. Two layers that work together

Once you accept that split, the architecture becomes cleaner. I think of it as two layers with a governed boundary between them.

The intelligence layer is where agents live, whether they are Joule agents, custom agents built on SAP BTP, or third-party agents. They understand the request, choose the right tools, interpret results, investigate exceptions and recommend or explain the next step.

The execution layer is SAP Integration Suite: Cloud Integration, API Management, Event Mesh, B2B and the connectivity into S/4HANA, ECC and third-party systems. It connects, transforms, routes, retries, secures and monitors.

An agent investigating a blocked invoice should never need to know how to reach the ERP, how to build the payload or which destination to use. It should ask for the evidence through an approved tool and spend its effort on explaining the discrepancy. The integration layer handles the rest.

Figure 1. Agents handle intent and reasoning; SAP Integration Suite provides governed access to business capabilities.

4. Why MCP matters here

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives compatible AI applications a standard way to discover and call tools. That sounds modest, but think about the alternative. Without a standard, every agent project discovers, interprets and rebuilds access to the same backends. The SAP deck compared it to a craftsperson. A good craftsperson is productive because trusted tools are already on the bench before the work starts. Agents need the same thing.

For a procurement agent, the bench might hold a handful of tools:

  • get_purchase_order to retrieve permitted PO details
  • check_approval_status to read the current approval state
  • validate_purchase_order to run defined validations
  • submit_for_approval to start an authorized approval workflow

Each tool has a clear purpose, a typed input and output contract, and narrow permissions. The agent picks the tool. The integration layer does the work.

One caution, because I hear this misunderstanding often: MCP standardizes the conversation between an agent and a tool. It does not make the tool secure, it does not check whether the user has authority to approve, and it does not guarantee the call succeeds. Those controls still live in the gateway, the integration logic and the backend.

5. Design tools for agents, not catalogs for agents

A typical SAP landscape has hundreds of APIs, iFlows and RFCs, many of them overlapping. The instinct is to expose all of them to the agent and let it figure things out. In my experience that is the fastest way to get an agent that is slow, expensive and unpredictable. Large tool catalogs make tool selection ambiguous, and oversized responses fill the context window with noise.

A lesson from one of my own programs: we built an AI assistant that answered purchase-order status questions for procurement and finance users, with a Vertex AI agent sitting behind Apigee X and calling into Ariba. Before it, these questions went into an email queue and often took a day to answer. After it, the answer came back in a few seconds. The model was not what made it work. What made it work was that the agent saw one narrow, well-described capability with a clean response, rather than the raw Ariba API surface. Most of the effort went into the API, not the prompt.

The same thinking applies to composition. Suppose an invoice-investigation agent needs invoice details, PO details and goods-receipt data. The naive design gives it three tools and asks it to correlate the responses. The better design composes them behind one business-oriented interface and returns a focused, structured result.

Figure 2. From multiple APIs to one agent-centric composed API.

This is now something SAP explicitly calls out: combining multiple backend APIs and exposing them as optimized MCP endpoints for agent consumption. The benefits are real (fewer tool calls, less correlation logic in the agent, smaller context, clearer ownership), but they are not free. Composition moves work into the integration layer, and its effect on latency and cost depends on data volumes, caching and how well you handle partial failures. Design it like any other API, with the same care.

The goal is not to expose more APIs to agents. It is to expose better business capabilities.

6. API-centric integration and the API artifact

Anyone who has worked on BTP for a while knows the split. Integration logic (routing, mapping, orchestration) lives in an iFlow in Cloud Integration. Exposure, security policies and throttling live in an API proxy in API Management. Two artifacts, two experiences, two places to look when something breaks.

API-centric integration introduces the API artifact, a single design and runtime element that combines the qualities of both: secure and publish, policy enforcement and throttling on one side; message routing, transformation and call orchestration on the other. It runs on the Integration Cell, a single runtime for Cloud Integration and API Management. According to the session, that removes extra hops and the double charging that came from passing a call through both. Monitoring is unified through the message processing log (MPL), with analytics feeding the existing API Management dashboards.

The capabilities that caught my attention as an architect:

  • Discovery of backend services from BTP destinations, the SAP Gateway catalog service for on-premise S/4HANA, and systems registered in the BTP cockpit's System Landscape.
  • API specifications attached as OpenAPI, or generated from natural language. A machine-readable spec is what lets an API be extended as an MCP tool, so this matters more than it looks.
  • Security with credentials scoped to a controlled set of APIs instead of master credentials, binding to XSUAA for token exchange across BTP, and principal propagation to on-premise systems. Validation of tokens from external OIDC issuers was shown as roadmap.
  • Developer Hub as one catalog where application developers subscribe to APIs and agents discover MCP servers, with self-registration for credentials.

On adoption, SAP's own recommendation was refreshingly conservative: consider the API artifact in the Integration Cell for greenfield projects, with no changes to existing deployments. I would put it this way:

  1. New work: design with the API artifact where the runtime and features you need are available.
  2. Stable integrations: leave them alone. A working iFlow that meets its SLA is not technical debt.
  3. Targeted modernization: consolidate when a flow is already being redesigned, or when a capability needs governed exposure to agents.
  4. Automation later: treat AI-assisted migration as something to evaluate once it is a supported capability, not something to plan budgets around today.

I have led enough migrations, from Oracle SOA 11g to 12c, from SOA to SAP BTP and from Boomi to Apigee X, to say this plainly: mass conversions without a business reason rarely pay back. Modernize where the change already touches.

7. Three paths to MCP with the MCP Gateway

This is the part I think matters most for SAP customers. The MCP Gateway in Integration Suite exposes your APIs, integrations and data sources as governed MCP servers. The session described three alternative starting points. They are options, not sequential steps.

Figure 3. Three paths to MCP enablement with SAP Integration Suite.

Path 1: from an API artifact. Expose a deployed API artifact's operations natively as MCP tools. This is the natural route for new API-centric work.

Path 2: from existing API specifications. Bring in specifications from existing API Management deployments or external HTTP endpoints. The technical spec is translated into MCP schema and enriched with natural-language semantics so agents can understand what each tool does.

Path 3: from RFCs. Expose remote-enabled function modules from ECC or S/4HANA. For a lot of customers this is the big one. Many core processes still run on ECC and on BAPIs that have been stable for fifteen years. Rebuilding every one of them as a new REST service before an agent can use it would delay adoption by years. That said, not every RFC should be agent-callable. Pick them deliberately, scope them tightly, and keep the backend authorization checks in place.

Two other points are worth noting. First, SAP Architecture Center now positions the MCP Gateway as the endorsed pathway for external third-party agents and for customer-built agents on BTP to reach SAP systems, with federation of third-party MCP servers on the roadmap. Second, MCP itself is still evolving quickly. If you run self-managed MCP servers, you own the job of tracking the specification and planning upgrades. A managed gateway takes that off your plate, which is a reasonable trade for most enterprise teams.

8. Guardrails are part of the design, not an add-on

In classic integration, it was usually enough to know that application X called API Y. With agents, you need to know which agent acted, on whose behalf, which tool it called, what authorization applied, and whether the business outcome was what everyone expected. Before any agent touches a transactional system, I want to see answers to these:

  • Identity and least privilege. Which agents and users can call which tools? Scoped credentials, not shared master keys.
  • Business authorization. Technical access must never bypass approval limits or segregation of duties. Being able to call submit_for_approval is not the same as being allowed to approve.
  • Input validation. Validate tool inputs against schema and business constraints before anything executes.
  • Traffic management. Rate limits, IP restrictions and payload protection, so a looping agent cannot flood an ECC system.
  • Error semantics. A rejected PO is a business outcome. An unreachable backend is a technical failure. The agent needs to be able to tell the difference.
  • Traceability. Enough logging to reconstruct a tool call end to end during an incident or an audit.
  • Human oversight. High-value or policy-sensitive actions go to a person. Design that path in from day one.

9. Context engineering is an integration concern

There is a common assumption that more context makes an agent smarter. Usually it does the opposite. Twenty overlapping tools and a 4,000-line payload make it harder for the model to choose correctly, and you pay for every token.

What works is focused tool descriptions, explicit input and output schemas, composed responses that contain only what the task needs, and retrieval on demand rather than up front. Notice that almost all of those are decisions made in the integration layer, not in the prompt. How well an agent behaves depends a great deal on what the surrounding architecture lets it see, reach and do.

10. Putting it together: invoice exception management

Here is how I would apply all of this to a scenario most SAP customers will recognize: thousands of supplier invoices a month, most of which match cleanly and a minority that do not.

Routine invoices never see an agent. Integration Suite ingests them, converts formats, runs the deterministic three-way match and posts them according to the rules. There is no reason to pay for reasoning on an invoice that matches.

Exceptions are where the agent comes in. When the match fails on a price variance, a missing goods receipt or a suspected duplicate, the agent calls a composed get_invoice_context tool, compares the evidence, explains the likely cause in plain language and recommends a next step.

Resolution stays controlled. The agent can trigger an authorized action within its limits or route a recommendation to an AP specialist. Either way, the integration layer validates the request and executes it with the normal controls.

Measurement decides whether it was worth it. I would track exception resolution time, the manual intervention rate, integration failure rate, cost per agent invocation and the share of cases resolved within policy. If those numbers do not move, the agent is a nice demo and nothing more.

11. A word on cost

Agent cost is not just tokens. It includes repeated tool calls, orchestration overhead, monitoring, governance and the time people spend investigating odd behavior. Keeping agents off deterministic steps is the single biggest lever. After that: reuse existing iFlows and APIs, keep responses small, compose where it saves calls, and measure consumption next to business outcomes. Edition requirements and AI-unit terms for these capabilities can change, so confirm current details with SAP before you build a business case.

Closing thoughts: orchestration, not universal agentization

The next phase of enterprise AI will not be won by the biggest model. It will be won by the teams that connect models to business processes without giving up the reliability, security and discipline that integration teams have spent years building.

If you are starting this week, here is what I would do:

  1. Take one end-to-end process, such as P2P, and score each step for reasoning value versus execution value.
  2. Pick one exception-heavy step where an agent clearly helps.
  3. Design two or three narrow, composed tools for it. Not twenty.
  4. Expose them through the MCP Gateway using whichever path fits: API artifact, existing spec or RFC.
  5. Put identity, authorization, rate limits and logging in place before go-live, and measure the outcome.

For those of us who have spent our careers in integration, this is good news. The skills that agentic AI needs most (clean contracts, governed access, reliable execution, good observability) are the ones we already have. Our job is not shrinking. It is moving one layer closer to the business.

I would like to hear how others are approaching this. Are you exposing RFCs to agents, or holding back until APIs are cleaner? Let me know in the comments.
